Operators must refresh the checkpoint when they can attest to continued collection; after 15 minutes its state is stale. Declared gaps are preserved across checkpoints. Restoring an unavailable source records its outage interval; a window overlapping a gap remains partial. Gaps wholly before an advanced retention floor can be retired. watermark is the declared snapshot-through instant, not a process observation or the last event in one page. Population and collection contract are included in every response.

Coverage states are missing (no declaration), unavailable (disabled source), stale, absent_history (window wholly before the served retention floor), partial (window crosses coverage/retention/watermark, or any best-effort gateway stream), and complete (covered transactional governance stream). A separate observation_state distinguishes recorded events from no recorded events. observed_count=0 alone never claims collection was complete. Sparse buckets represent recorded events only: missing buckets are not synthesized zeros. Phase 14 adds server-computed distinct verified clients, finite reported latency samples and declared access-decision counts, while leaving event/CSV payloads content-free. Counts, buckets and details use one MongoDB pre-aggregation visibility predicate, within one snapshot serialized with policy revocation. A page length is never a total. Timezone changes bucket boundaries, not stored event instants.

Overview aggregate data has a bounded process cache: at most 128 results and 4 MiB of encoded result payload per policy engine/source, with a 30-second maximum lifetime. Keys bind organization, subject, exact action/resource visibility, policy revision, retention and all query filters. A MongoDB change stream is opened before the first data snapshot and drained before reuse. Inserts (including late ones) invalidate their own organization's results; edits/deletions without a known prior owner conservatively invalidate the source. Observer generations are bounded to 512 organizations. Interrupted observation discards the cache and refuses reuse. Overlapping identical computations share bounded work. These are cached MongoDB aggregates, not persistent historical rollups or cached authority. generated_at retains the original observation time.

Every response reauthorizes current membership, ancestry and visibility, fences the policy anchor, then checks natural grant expiry synchronously after the last await. Cold overview aggregation has a ten-second database ceiling; ordinary detail/report operations retain their three-second ceiling. Cold latency and warm-cache latency must be measured separately. The cache has no disk, backup, outbox, browser-storage or credential payload. Its change-stream cursor belongs to the database client and requires MongoDB change-stream read permission.

Summary routes authenticate the browser and bind an identity-only principal with no corpus grants. Their services obtain fresh transactional policy snapshots for the actual metadata action and resources. The three directory list routes (members, teams, team members) similarly use their directory service's fresh action-specific snapshot and database predicate. Other domain routes retain their normal corpus policy boundary. Headers/body fields cannot select this server-owned route behavior or turn an empty policy into ALL.

The served retention floor applies to detail, aggregate and downloads even when installation archives retain older events. Physical deletion/archive retention remains explicitly installation_managed; Phase 8 does not claim an automatic governance TTL or tenant backup/restore. Whole-database backups and raw shared metrics remain operator-only.

Reports and operational bounds

reports:export on the organization is additionally required. The fixed Phase 5 catalog allows owner/admin/auditor export assignments; an executive aggregate assignment or a team lead role alone cannot export. Creation requires CSRF, Origin and recent MFA. Downloads require the same recipient, active browser session, recent MFA, unchanged policy/membership revision, current source visibility and an unexpired five-minute descriptor. Revocation/reinstatement or widening cannot resurrect an old report. Links grant no bearer authority. Current retention can further narrow a previously requested report.

Reports are synchronous because their work is bounded: at most 5,000 rows and 2 MiB UTF-8 CSV, with a three-second MongoDB operation deadline and no disk spilling. Overflow refuses delivery; it never silently returns the first page. Narrow the time/filter window. CSV quoting and formula neutralization cover =, +, -, @ after whitespace/control/BOM prefixes. Download headers include X-Summary-Metadata (source, window, timezone, observed population/count and coverage), no-store, nosniff and a fixed attachment filename. No persisted report payload, async job or downloadable temporary file is needed at these bounds. These are limits, not measured production performance results.

The focused real gate runs in disposable MongoDB using matching project/client IDs in both organizations. Use scripts/test-v6-summaries.sh for prerequisites plus Phase 8, or V6_SUMMARIES_DEVELOPMENT_ONLY=1 scripts/test-v6-isolation.sh for the complete two new integration files on independent disposable stacks. Neither command reads deployment credentials or sends real mail.

docs/backup.mdPublic documentation

Public documentation snapshot. Use the generated tool/API reference for contracts in this checkout and live capability discovery for your running deployment.

Backup and recovery

Written for whoever will restore this platform, probably in a hurry, possibly at night, possibly without having read this before.

The short version. MongoDB is the only thing that must survive. Take a daily backup, keep 7 daily / 4 weekly / 3 monthly, and prove once a week that one actually restores. The disaster-recovery procedure is at the end.

What has to be backed up, and what does not

Backed up Why
MongoDB — skills, chunks, project context, memories, creator/content records, research projects, sources, snapshots, documents, chunks, notes, claims, citations, briefs, candidates, promotion events, ingestion jobs, projects, API keys, audit log Yes The platform's only primary state. Nothing else can reconstruct it.
Vector embeddings Yes They live inside the documents, so they come along — and that is deliberate. Regenerating them means running the embedding model over every chunk again: minutes to hours of CPU for something already computed.
Search indexes (all configured mongot indexes) No Derived state. contextctl skills reindex rebuilds them from the documents in seconds to minutes.
The embedding model files No Re-downloaded, or placed on the volume out of band for an air-gapped host.
Secrets (secrets/, .env) Separately, by your secret manager Not in a database backup, and never in the same place as one.

The two rules worth stating plainly, because they pull in opposite directions and it is easy to get one of them backwards:

  • Search indexes are not a source of truth. Never restore from them, and never treat a healthy index as evidence the data is intact. They are a rebuildable projection of MongoDB.
  • Vectors are not an index. They are data, they are expensive, and they are in the backup. A restore does not re-embed anything.

So a restore is: bring MongoDB back, then rebuild the indexes. Never the other way around, and never only the first half.

Where backups live

BACKUP_DIRECTORY, ./backups by default. The directory is created 0700 and every file in it 0600 — an archive is every document the deployment holds, in one file, so the protection it gets is the protection the whole platform gets.

Under Compose it is a host directory bind-mounted at /backups, not a named volume, so you can copy backups off the machine with cp or rsync without going through Docker. The container writes as uid 999, so create it once:

mkdir -p backups
sudo chown 999:999 backups
chmod 700 backups

Point BACKUP_HOST_DIRECTORY somewhere else — another disk, a mounted share — if the backups should not live beside the data they protect.

Do not put it anywhere the platform serves. Not under a web root, not in a volume mounted into a container that answers requests, not in the repository. It is not in the image, and .gitignore covers the default path. If you ship backups off the host — and you should, a backup on the same disk survives a deleted collection but not a dead disk — send them somewhere with the same protection: private, encrypted at rest, and not the same failure domain.

Each backup is two files:

backups/
  context-20260916-131532.archive.gz     # mongodump archive, gzipped
  context-20260916-131532.manifest.json  # what it contains, and its checksum

The timestamp is UTC and fixed-width, so sorting by name is sorting by time, and the instant a backup was taken travels with it — a file copied to another host still expires on the right day, which a modification time would not.

The manifest records the database, the byte count, the SHA-256 of the archive, and the document count of every collection. That last one is what makes a restore checkable rather than assumed: a restore that reports success and leaves skills empty has failed, and only the counts would say so.

Taking a backup

docker compose exec -T context-api python -m app.cli.contextctl backup

Inside the platform, because a backup reaches MongoDB directly and under Compose MongoDB is on an internal network with no host port. And python -m app.cli.contextctl rather than contextctl, because the image installs the application's dependencies but not the project itself.

That one command dumps the database, writes the manifest, verifies the checksum and dry-run restore plan, and only then applies retention. A failed new archive is removed and cannot evict a known older backup. The archive is written under a temporary name and moved into place only when it is complete, so an interrupted backup never becomes one a restore might later choose.

# Keep this one regardless of retention.
… contextctl backup --no-prune

# A one-off copy before a risky migration: exactly where you said, no manifest,
# not part of the retained set, so it cannot push a real backup out of it.
… contextctl backup --output ./before-migration.archive.gz

Retention

The default keeps the newest backup of each of:

  • the last 7 days
  • the last 4 ISO weeks
  • the last 3 months

Tiers overlap rather than add up — today's backup is the newest of its day, its week and its month, and is kept once — so the default holds at most fourteen files and reaches back about three months.

Counted in periods, not files. "Seven daily" means the seven most recent days that have a backup. A rule counting files would, after one afternoon of six manual backups, hold six from that afternoon and one from yesterday; and a week of downtime would not silently expire everything that survived it.

BACKUP_RETAIN_DAILY=7
BACKUP_RETAIN_WEEKLY=4
BACKUP_RETAIN_MONTHLY=3

Setting all three to zero is refused at startup rather than on the night it would have deleted everything. A backup dated in the future — a clock that went backwards, a file copied from another host — is never deleted.

… contextctl backups list              # what you have, and what keeps each one
… contextctl backups prune --dry-run   # what retention would remove, and why
… contextctl backups prune

Verifying

Three levels, each stronger and more expensive:

# 1. The file is intact: it matches the checksum written with it.
# 2. mongorestore can open and plan it (--dryRun: writes nothing).
… contextctl backups verify
… contextctl backups verify --all

# 3. It actually restores. Into throwaway collections, counts compared with
#    the manifest, copies removed afterwards — win or lose.
… contextctl backups verify --restore

verify exits non-zero if any backup fails, so a scheduler can alert on it.

Only the third proves anything about recovery. SHA-256 detects byte-level truncation or corruption, and the dry run validates the restore plan; neither can say every document materializes. A backup that has never been restored is not yet known to be a backup — which is why the shipped schedule runs --restore weekly.

It restores into throwaway collections inside the application's own database, named restorecheck_<timestamp>_<nonce>__<collection>, and removes them afterwards whether the check passed or not. Into the same database rather than a separate one because the application authenticates as a user with readWrite on its own database and nothing else — restoring elsewhere would mean granting the platform cluster-wide privileges it deliberately does not have. Nothing live is touched: no real collection has that name, and the check never passes --drop, so it cannot write over what it is verifying. It does temporarily need disk for a second copy of the data.

Scheduling

Daily backups and a weekly restore check, as systemd timers:

sudo cp deploy/systemd/agent-context-backup.{service,timer} /etc/systemd/system/
sudo cp deploy/systemd/agent-context-backup-verify.{service,timer} /etc/systemd/system/
# The units run as `agent-context` from /opt/agent-context-platform. Change
# both to match your deployment, or override with `systemctl edit`.
sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl enable --now agent-context-backup.timer
sudo systemctl enable --now agent-context-backup-verify.timer

systemctl list-timers 'agent-context-*'
journalctl -u agent-context-backup.service -n 50

Persistent=true means a backup missed while the host was off is taken when it comes back, rather than skipped to tomorrow. RandomizedDelaySec keeps several hosts from starting at the same instant.

Cron instead, if you prefer:

17 2 * * *  cd /opt/agent-context-platform && ./scripts/backup.sh >> /var/log/agent-context-backup.log 2>&1
40 4 * * 0  cd /opt/agent-context-platform && docker compose exec -T context-api python -m app.cli.contextctl backups verify --restore

Alert on the job not running at all, not only on it failing. A backup timer that quietly stops firing produces no errors, and you find out when you need a backup. systemctl list-timers shows the last and next elapse.

Disaster recovery

The full procedure, in order. Each step is checked before the next, because a recovery that skips a check is a recovery you find out about later.

1. Stop the affected services

docker compose stop context-api mongot

Stop the API first so nothing writes while the database is being replaced, and mongot so it is not indexing a database that is about to change underneath it. Leave mongodb running — the restore needs it.

2. Restore MongoDB

docker compose run --rm --no-deps -T context-api \
  python -m app.cli.contextctl backups list
RESTORE_CONFIRMED=1 ./scripts/restore.sh --latest

The script uses a one-off container, not the stopped API container, so no request-serving process starts during recovery. It verifies the manifest, target database, checksum, byte count, and archive readability before passing --drop; afterwards it compares every restored collection count with the manifest. Any mismatch is a failure, not a warning.

Restoring a specific managed backup instead: RESTORE_CONFIRMED=1 ./scripts/restore.sh --name context-20260916-131532.archive.gz. Copy an external archive and its manifest into the configured backup directory before recovery so it receives the same integrity and collection checks.

3. Verify the replica set

docker compose exec -T mongodb /usr/local/bin/mongodb-healthcheck.sh

Exit status zero means the authenticated replica-set check found this member primary. Nothing below works until it is: the platform requires a primary for transactions, and mongot replicates from it.

4. Verify the collections

docker compose run --rm --no-deps -T context-api \
  python -m app.cli.contextctl --json backups list \
  | jq '.backups[0] | {backup, documents, collection_counts}'

Keep this output with the recovery record. The restore already compared these manifest counts with the live database and would have exited non-zero if a skill, project, project-context item, memory, research source/snapshot/document/chunk, research note/claim/citation/brief/candidate/promotion event/ingestion job, API key, or audit record was missing.

5. Verify the indexes

docker compose run --rm --no-deps -T context-api \
  python -m app.cli.contextctl skills reindex --database-only

At this point mongot is intentionally still stopped. This verifies/reconciles the MongoDB collection validators and standard indexes without contacting the search coordinator. Do not continue on an error.

6. Start mongot

docker compose start mongot
docker compose ps mongot

Wait for the Compose health state to become healthy before rebuilding search.

7. Verify search

docker compose run --rm --no-deps -T context-api \
  python -m app.cli.contextctl skills reindex

Search indexes are not in the backup. reindex recreates or reconciles every configured index against the restored documents and loaded local model. It is idempotent. A new index can remain BUILDING; repeat the command until every index reports unchanged, then prove queries work in the step 11 smoke tests.

8. Verify embeddings

docker compose run --rm --no-deps -T context-api python -c '
import asyncio
from app.core.config import get_settings
from app.db.client import MongoDBClient

async def verify():
    settings = get_settings()
    client = MongoDBClient(settings)
    await client.connect(require_search=False)
    try:
        for name in ("skill_chunks", "project_context", "memories"):
            query = {"embedding": {"$exists": True},
                     "embedding_dimensions": settings.embedding_dimensions}
            print(name, await client.database[name].count_documents(query))
    finally:
        await client.close()

asyncio.run(verify())'

Compare the non-zero counts with the pre-disaster inventory for collections that had embeddings. Nothing should need re-embedding: vectors were in the backup. If dimensions do not match, the deployment's EMBEDDING_MODEL changed since the backup — fix the setting rather than regenerating data implicitly.

9. Start the API

docker compose start context-api
curl --fail http://127.0.0.1:8000/health/ready

Readiness is the final index-state check: it requires MongoDB, mongot, the embedding model, and all six search indexes to be queryable.

10. Start MCP

The MCP server is spawned by its client, so there is nothing to start. Confirm one can talk to the platform:

docker compose --profile mcp run --rm -T mcp <<< \
  '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"initialize","params":{"protocolVersion":"2024-11-05","capabilities":{},"clientInfo":{"name":"smoke","version":"1"}}}'

If the API requires a key, the server needs one — see security.md.

11. Run smoke tests

Retrieval is the thing the platform exists to do, so it is the last thing checked:

K=$(cat ./secrets/codex-api-key)

# A skill, a project's context, and a memory all reachable, ranked together.
curl --fail -H "Authorization: Bearer $K" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"query":"idempotency","project_id":"payment-service","limit":5}' \
  http://127.0.0.1:8000/api/v1/search | jq '.results[] | {source, title}'

# Each source individually, so a missing one is obvious.
curl --fail -H "Authorization: Bearer $K" http://127.0.0.1:8000/api/v1/skills | jq '.items | length'
curl --fail -H "Authorization: Bearer $K" \
  'http://127.0.0.1:8000/api/v1/context?project_id=payment-service' | jq '.items | length'
curl --fail -H "Authorization: Bearer $K" http://127.0.0.1:8000/api/v1/memory | jq '.items | length'

A search that returns results from every expected source is the point at which the recovery is done. Anything less and something in steps 4–8 did not hold.

Onto a clean host

The same procedure, with the platform built first:

  1. Install Docker with Compose v2.
  2. Clone the repository; restore secrets/ and .env from your secret manager.
  3. ./scripts/prepare-docker-wheels.sh && docker compose up -d --build --wait
  4. Copy the backup onto the host, into BACKUP_HOST_DIRECTORY.
  5. contextctl backups verify --name <backup> before relying on it.
  6. Continue from step 1 above.

What to check before you need this

  • contextctl backups list shows a backup from today.
  • systemctl list-timers 'agent-context-*' shows a next elapse in the future.
  • The most recent backups verify --restore passed, and you know when.
  • The backups exist somewhere that is not this host.
  • Someone other than you has followed this document end to end, once.

Reference

Setting Default Meaning
BACKUP_HOST_DIRECTORY ./backups Host directory mounted into the container; create it owned by uid 999 with mode 0700.
BACKUP_DIRECTORY /backups under Compose Container path where backups are written. Created/tightened to 0700.
BACKUP_RETAIN_DAILY 7 Days of daily backups to keep.
BACKUP_RETAIN_WEEKLY 4 ISO weeks to keep.
BACKUP_RETAIN_MONTHLY 3 Months to keep.
BACKUP_TIMEOUT_SECONDS 3600 How long one tool invocation may take.
Command Does
contextctl backup Take one, write its manifest, apply retention
contextctl backup --no-prune Take one and keep everything
contextctl backup --output PATH One-off to a path; unmanaged
contextctl backups list What you have, and what keeps each one
contextctl backups verify Checksum and readability of the newest
contextctl backups verify --all …of every backup
contextctl backups verify --restore Prove it restores, into throwaway collections
contextctl backups prune --dry-run What retention would remove, and why
contextctl backups prune Apply retention
contextctl restore --latest --yes Restore the newest
contextctl restore --name N --yes Restore a named one
contextctl restore --input PATH --yes Restore from a path

scripts/backup.sh and scripts/restore.sh wrap these for a scheduler. The restore script refuses to run without RESTORE_CONFIRMED=1, and prints the steps it does not do.

V6 management and encryption-key recovery

Whole-installation archives include every enumerated collection: private users/identities/password hashes/MFA, browser sessions and challenges, memberships, teams/invitations, policy anchors/grants/governance audit/outbox, client custody, credential delivery metadata, jobs, summary coverage/reports and adoption preservation/quarantine. No tenant role or CSV export grants this capability. Raw archives are not exposed by /console, /api/v6, MCP or the marketing site.

Use stopped writers for exact count-and-dump rehearsals; an online database-level dump is not a transactional multi-collection snapshot claim. Scratch restore verification compares per-collection inventories as well as combined counts, and never passes --drop. A tenant report cannot be supplied as a managed backup.

Managed manifests record SHA-256 commitments to every retained mounted MFA key version without recording any key bytes. Restore verification and managed restore require the matching keyring; the same key ID with different bytes is refused. Keep encrypted off-host recovery copies of that keyring, database credentials, TLS key and approved IdP registrations separately, under operator controls. Local passwords and opaque browser session hashes are database state, not external plaintext password/session-signing files. Recover MFA/PKCE keys before opening identity services; password reset cannot recover encrypted factors. Old manifests without commitments remain readable, but require a separate decryption rehearsal.

The disposable V6 recovery test materializes all collections, compares original BSON and decrypts a restored factor with a recovered keyring. This does not prove production recovery until repeated against your own preserved secrets and data. The optional Keycloak PostgreSQL database, provider keys and configuration need their own consistent backup/recovery; MongoDB cannot recover that IdP. See console deployment for the TLS/cutover and provider runbooks. After restoring an older policy snapshot, revoke sessions/keys/challenges and repeat operator activation checks before admitting traffic.

docs/cli.mdPublic documentation

Public documentation snapshot. Use the generated tool/API reference for contracts in this checkout and live capability discovery for your running deployment.

contextctl

The operator's interface to the platform. Codex reaches it through MCP and an application reaches it through the API; contextctl is how a person does.

contextctl health
contextctl search "how do we prevent duplicate payments?" --project-id payment-service
contextctl --json memory search "typing conventions" | jq .results

Every command is a thin translation: parse arguments, call one service or one endpoint, print the result. Nothing here ranks, embeds, or decides what a project may see.

Two kinds of command

The difference is visible in what each one needs, and it is not arbitrary.

Command Reaches Because
skills list the API it is a read the API already serves
projects create, projects list the API same
creator show, creator update, creator pillars the API profile authorization and optimistic updates live there
content ideas, content idea create, content brief, content novelty, content repurpose, content export the API discovery, provenance, authorization, and platform formatting live there
search, memory search the API retrieval lives behind it; a second copy would drift
health the API readiness is the API's own answer
skills import MongoDB no endpoint exposes it, and only an operator should do it
skills reindex MongoDB + mongot same
keys create, keys list, keys revoke MongoDB operator bootstrap and key administration require private database access
keys scopes nothing it describes the platform's own vocabulary
backup, restore, backups MongoDB same, and the tools run beside it

So a search never fails for want of MongoDB credentials, and an import never fails for want of an API address. Each command reads only the configuration it actually uses.

It also decides where you run it. The API publishes a port, so the commands that ask it run from anywhere. MongoDB does not — under Compose it is on an internal network — so the commands that reach it run inside the platform:

docker compose exec -T context-api python -m app.cli.contextctl keys list
docker compose run --rm context-api python -m app.cli.contextctl skills import

python -m app.cli.contextctl rather than contextctl: the image installs the application's dependencies but not the project, so the console script exists only where you have run pip install -e .. The syntax below is written bare for readability; prefix it accordingly.

Commands

skills

contextctl skills list [--status active] [--category backend] [--tag python] [--limit 20]
contextctl skills import [--directory ./skills] [--no-embeddings]
contextctl skills reindex [--no-embeddings]

import is idempotent: unchanged content is a no-op, changed content under the same version is refused, and a new version supersedes the previous one while keeping its history.

reindex reconciles all six search indexes. They are derived state — not backed up, always rebuildable — so this is what you run after a restore, or after changing the embedding model. It is idempotent; a healthy deployment reports unchanged. With --no-embeddings it rebuilds the three lexical indexes alone, which is what you want when the model is unavailable but search should still work.

skill proposals

contextctl skill proposal list --research-project-id retry-evidence [--skill-id backend-guidance]
contextctl skill proposal show --research-project-id retry-evidence --proposal-id idempotency-guidance
contextctl skill proposal export --research-project-id retry-evidence --proposal-id idempotency-guidance

These are read/export-only clients for generated skill-update proposals. export prints the stored Markdown patch for a separate human review process; it does not write canonical Markdown, call Git, or invoke the skill importer.

projects

contextctl projects create --project-id payment-service --name "Payment Service" \
  --description "Card and wallet payments" \
  --repository git@example.invalid:sampleco/payment-service.git \
  --environment production --tag payments
contextctl projects list [--limit 20] [--cursor …]

The identifier is permanent: it derives the document key, so it cannot be taken twice and nothing moves between projects.

project bindings

contextctl project binding add --project-id payment-service --type git_remote \
  --value git@github.com:example/payment-service.git
contextctl project binding list [--project-id payment-service] [--limit 20] [--cursor …]
contextctl project binding delete payment-remote --revision 1

Bindings are the explicit deterministic mapping from a local repository or workspace hint to a V1 project. Repository remotes are normalized without any network or filesystem access, so standard SSH and HTTPS forms identify the same repository. Creating a duplicate is refused; a mapping already owned by another project is a conflict. Deletion requires the revision shown by list, so an operator cannot silently remove a binding another operator changed.

search

contextctl search "Implement payment refund support." --project-id payment-service
contextctl search "wallet:read" --source active_skill --limit 3
contextctl search "refund rules" --project-id payment-service --content

Skills, the project's own recorded context, and memory searched together and ranked against each other. --content prints each result in full; without it you get the ranking and what it cost.

Naming no project excludes project context and project memory. Organization-global knowledge remains eligible only with its explicit resource policy; a client-linked credential can also search its own operational agent memory. Projects are requested explicitly and never inferred.

memory

contextctl memory search "typing conventions"
contextctl memory search "refund review" --project-id payment-service
contextctl memory search "deploys" --status superseded

Naming a project searches its authorized memory and permitted organization-global memory together. Archived and superseded memory is excluded unless asked for.

health

contextctl health          # is the platform ready?
contextctl health --live   # is the process alive?

Exits 3 when the platform is not ready, so a deployment script can gate on it:

contextctl health || exit 1

creator

contextctl creator show --profile-id personal-brand
contextctl creator update --profile-id personal-brand --expected-revision 2 \
  --status inactive --audience "software architects"
contextctl creator pillars --profile-id personal-brand --limit 20

Creator commands are API clients. They never read MongoDB directly and creator preference data is never treated as hidden system instructions. update sends only named fields and requires the revision read from show, so a concurrent update is refused rather than replaced.

content

contextctl content ideas --profile-id personal-brand --project-id payment-service \
  --pillar-id payments --platform linkedin --since 2026-09-01T00:00:00Z
contextctl content idea create --profile-id personal-brand --idea-id payment-idempotency \
  --title "Idempotent payment retries" --description "Explain the stored retry rule." \
  --platform linkedin --origin-type project_context --origin-source-id 0123456789abcdef01234567 \
  --project-id payment-service --priority 0.9
contextctl content brief --profile-id personal-brand --idea-id payment-idempotency --platform medium
contextctl content novelty --profile-id personal-brand --title "Monitoring Outbox lag" \
  --description "Explain alerting and exhausted retries." --tag outbox --project-id payment-service
contextctl content repurpose --profile-id personal-brand --content-id outbox-medium \
  --target linkedin --target github
contextctl content export --profile-id personal-brand --content-id outbox-medium --mode markdown
contextctl content export --profile-id personal-brand --content-id architecture-readme \
  --mode file --output ./README.md

content ideas prints source-backed candidate topics and saves nothing. content idea create is the explicit reviewed write, including all cited origin IDs. content brief prepares an evidence package and saves nothing; it does not generate a draft or publish a result. These commands call the V2 API only, so profile/project authorization and provenance checks remain centralized.

content novelty prints advisory, explainable overlap with only history that the caller may access. content repurpose prints platform-specific source and skill planning fields, never a generated body or saved draft. Both also call only the V2 API.

content export calls the API to authorize, validate, and format one existing content item. stdout and markdown print the returned representation. file requires an explicit --output PATH and writes UTF-8 only on the local CLI host; an existing file is refused unless --force is also passed. This is a manual export, never an external publish. See content-export.md for platform representations and safety rules.

research

contextctl research create --research-project-id retry-evidence --name "Retry evidence" \
  --question "What constrains safe payment retries?" --type technical_research \
  --related-project-id payment-service
contextctl research search --research-project-id retry-evidence --query "idempotency retry"
contextctl research search --research-project-id repository-evidence --query "authenticate" \
  --retrieval-profile research_code --method lexical
contextctl source ingest --source-id payments-repository --fetch-repository
contextctl research brief --research-project-id retry-evidence --brief-id retry-summary \
  --scope "Provider documentation and incident reports" \
  --next-question "Which SDK versions enforce the retry requirement?"

contextctl source ingest --fetch-repository sends only the registered source identifier; it does not take a repository URL, path, ref, credentials, or command. The server’s Git provider applies the public-HTTPS, size, and read-only execution controls.

contextctl research brief asks the API to persist structured claim, citation, source, contradiction, uncertainty, and next-question references. It does not generate prose, select a side of conflicting evidence, claim completeness, fetch a source, or promote any result into memory, project context, or a skill.

candidate

contextctl candidate list --research-project-id retry-evidence --status pending_review
contextctl candidate approve --research-project-id retry-evidence --candidate-id retry-context \
  --expected-revision 1 --reason "Reviewed retained evidence"
contextctl candidate reject --research-project-id retry-evidence --candidate-id retry-context \
  --expected-revision 1 --needs-changes --reason "Narrow the target statement"

Candidates retain the exact claim and citation IDs that motivated a proposal. approve and reject are explicit review decisions only: they create an immutable decision event, but never write V1 memory, project context, skills, or content. --needs-changes is a rejection-path review state, not a promotion.

Promote an explicitly approved candidate through the authorized V1 target:

contextctl candidate promote \
  --research-project-id retry-evidence \
  --candidate-id retry-context \
  --expected-revision 2 \
  --supersedes-context-id 0123456789abcdef01234567

The optional --supersedes-context-id is only for project-context promotion. The server requires the appropriate V1 target write scope, creates the replacement first, marks that explicit old context superseded, retains evidence provenance on the new target, and refuses skill changes.

keys

contextctl keys scopes describes the bearer action vocabulary without database access. Other key commands require explicit --org-id and private installation operator credentials. Legacy issuance is refused under managed policy; it is not a way to bypass approved client policy or recipient-only delivery.

For managed installations approve the client/sponsor envelope, then have the recipient authenticate and generate a credential once through the console/API. Leads cannot recover that token. Retry gives safe metadata, and lost delivery needs revoke/replacement. See managed agents.

contextctl keys scopes
contextctl --org-id YOUR_ORG keys list --status active --limit 20
contextctl --org-id YOUR_ORG keys revoke --key-id PUBLIC_KEY_ID

The historical pre-management command is contextctl --org-id YOUR_ORG keys create. Its legacy omitted project/profile arrays mean reviewed explicit all_in_org inside the adoption organization only; managed NONE is never serialized that way. Do not use a legacy create example for human or managed-machine provisioning. Revocation retains historical records/provenance. Current authority is checked again on requests and MCP preflight, not just at process connection time.

backup, restore, and backups

contextctl backup                        # into the configured directory, with retention
contextctl backup --no-prune             # keep this one regardless of retention
contextctl backup --output ./one-off.archive.gz   # a path you named; unmanaged

contextctl backups list
contextctl backups verify [--all] [--restore]
contextctl backups prune [--dry-run]

contextctl restore --latest --drop --yes
contextctl restore --name context-20260916-131532.archive.gz --yes
contextctl restore --input ./one-off.archive.gz --yes

A bare backup writes into BACKUP_DIRECTORY, records a manifest beside the archive, and applies the retention policy — 7 daily, 4 weekly, 3 monthly by default. --output is the unmanaged form: a one-off copy before a risky migration, which should not join the retained set and push a real backup out of it.

backups verify checks the archive against the checksum written with it and that mongorestore can read it. --restore goes further and actually restores it into throwaway collections, comparing the document counts with the manifest — the only check that proves a backup restores. It exits non-zero if any backup fails, so a scheduler can alert on it.

See backup.md for the strategy, the scheduling, and the disaster-recovery procedure.

Search indexes are not backed up. They are derived state that contextctl skills reindex rebuilds from the stored documents, and treating them as a backup would be treating a cache as a record. The restore output says so.

restore requires --yes. It is not a prompt — it stays scriptable — but nothing overwrites a database because a command was typed with one word missing. --drop replaces each collection rather than merging into it.

The full procedure:

  1. Stop the API.
  2. contextctl restore --input … --drop --yes
  3. contextctl skills reindex
  4. Start the API.
  5. contextctl health

The production and test images include the matching MongoDB Database Tools, so the CLI and mongodump/mongorestore coexist without publishing MongoDB. Take scheduled backups in the running API container. Run a disaster restore through scripts/restore.sh, which uses a one-off container while the serving API remains stopped. A managed restore verifies the manifest, checksum, archive readability, target database, and restored collection counts.

Output

Human-readable by default, --json for anything that will be parsed:

contextctl --json health | jq '.failing'
contextctl --json search "refunds" --project-id payment-service | jq '.results[].title'

--json is a global flag and goes before the command. Results go to stdout and failures to stderr, both as JSON when --json is set, so a failure never lands in the pipe:

{ "error": "the platform is unreachable", "exit_code": 3, "hint": "… contextctl health" }

Nothing is interactive. Every command runs unattended.

Exit codes

Code Meaning
0 the command succeeded
1 the command ran and did not succeed — a record was absent, a write conflicted
2 the arguments were wrong
3 the platform could not be reached, or is not ready

1 and 3 are deliberately different: one means the command was wrong, the other means nothing is listening. A retry loop should retry 3 and give up on 1.

Configuration

Through the environment, like everything else.

Variable Purpose Default
CONTEXTCTL_API_BASE_URL where the Context API listens http://127.0.0.1:8000
CONTEXTCTL_API_TOKEN_FILE file holding a bearer token unset
CONTEXTCTL_API_TOKEN the token inline; prefer the file unset
CONTEXTCTL_REQUEST_TIMEOUT_SECONDS per-request timeout 30
MONGODB_* only for import, reindex, keys, backup, restore see deployment.md

--api-base-url and --timeout override the first and last for one invocation.

The CLI settings are separate from the MCP server's on purpose: an operator's terminal and an agent's tool server are different callers, and pointing one at another deployment should not move the other.

Secrets

No command accepts a password or a token as an argument, and a test asserts that none ever grows one. Both are read from the environment or from a file, because argv is readable by every process on the host through /proc and ends up in shell history and CI logs. keys create prints a key rather than taking one, which is the same rule from the other side.

Prefer CONTEXTCTL_API_TOKEN_FILE over CONTEXTCTL_API_TOKEN for the same reason.

backup and restore pass the MongoDB password to the database tools through a private configuration file, created at mode 0600 before anything is written to it and removed when the command finishes. It is never in argv, never in their environment, and never printed.

Troubleshooting

this command needs the platform's database settings, and they are not set — you ran a MongoDB-reaching command (skills import, skills reindex, keys, backup, restore) from the host. The local ignored .env is written for Compose, which maps MONGODB_APP_USERNAME to the MONGODB_USERNAME the application reads — so the file that looks like it configures everything configures a different set of names. And under Compose the database is on an internal network with no host port, so it is unreachable from the host anyway. Run these inside the platform:

docker compose exec -T context-api python -m app.cli.contextctl keys list

python -m app.cli.contextctl rather than contextctl: the image installs the application's dependencies but not the project, so the console script is not in it.

the platform is unreachable — nothing is listening at CONTEXTCTL_API_BASE_URL. Check the address and that the API is up. The CLI deliberately ignores inherited HTTP_PROXY, HTTPS_PROXY, and ALL_PROXY values because the self-hosted API address is explicit.

the platform is not ready — the API answered but a capability is failing. The message names which; contextctl --json health | jq .failing lists them.

mongodump was not found — the MongoDB Database Tools are not on PATH. Run the command in the mongodb container, as above.

skills list is empty — skills are imported, not seeded: contextctl skills import.

A search returns nothing right after a write — mongot indexes asynchronously, usually within a second. If it persists, contextctl health will say whether the index is queryable.

the arguments were rejected as invalid — the API refused the request, and its own message follows. --scope project without --project-id is the common one.

Installing

The console script is declared in pyproject.toml, so an editable install puts contextctl on PATH:

pip install -e .
contextctl --help

Without installing, it runs as a module:

python -m app.cli.contextctl --help

Verification

python -m pytest                                     # parsing, execution, exit codes, JSON
docker compose --profile test run --rm --build test  # live mongod + mongot checks

Parsing is tested against the full command tree — every required command, every refusal, and that no command has grown a secret-bearing flag. Execution is tested by running whole invocations in-process against a recording HTTP double, which is what makes the exit codes themselves assertable. Backup and restore run a real subprocess so the claim about the process table is proved rather than asserted.

docs/client-onboarding.mdPublic documentation

Public documentation snapshot. Use the generated tool/API reference for contracts in this checkout and live capability discovery for your running deployment.

Generic MCP client onboarding

Managed installation setup

Complete the organization console cutovers first. A lead approves bounded client policy and verified sponsor/team; the authenticated recipient generates their token once. Do not use a legacy operator key recipe to bypass managed issuance. Leads cannot recover another worker's plaintext. Copy explicitly into a private file/approved secret store; retries return metadata and lost delivery needs revoke/replacement. Never store a token in source or browser local/session storage.

Each credential is bound to one organization. Key/client policy intersects current sponsor, team and delegation rights per action/resource in REST and every MCP preflight, including active sessions. Browser cookies cannot authenticate this bearer surface. Provider API keys remain separate. Template edits/disable do not change assigned clients or keys. See managed agents for rotation, expiry, custody, revocation and normal-machine review refusal.

Agent Context has one capability-based MCP gateway and one shared knowledge store. Adding a compatible client is an administrative identity-and-configuration task, not a request for a client-specific backend, database, search tool, or authorization implementation.

Supported integration metadata

List the built-in adapters:

contextctl integration list
contextctl integration show codex
contextctl integration show claude-code
contextctl integration show gemini-cli
contextctl integration show custom

show emits only token-free configuration references, compatibility facts, and verification steps. It never creates a client, issues a credential, edits a client configuration file, or makes a network request.

The built-in adapters cover Codex's existing stdio launcher, Claude Code's remote HTTP configuration, Gemini CLI's Streamable HTTP settings, and a vendor-neutral custom Streamable HTTP template. All use the existing tools and gateway controls.

Historical unmanaged administration

The following V4 commands apply only to an explicitly unmanaged rehearsal. They are refused by managed policy and are not the current evaluation setup path. For the evaluation use staged commissioning, independent client approval and recipient-only delivery above.

An operator creates the client identity and grants only the necessary scopes and projects. For example, a custom Streamable HTTP client can start with a read-only capability set:

contextctl agent create \
  --client-id review-agent \
  --type custom \
  --name "Review agent" \
  --owner-id YOUR_OWNER_ID \
  --scope skills:read \
  --scope projects:read \
  --scope context:read \
  --scope memory:read \
  --scope search:read \
  --scope agent:self \
  --project payment-service

contextctl agent token create review-agent

Credential issuance is administrative. The gateway never exposes a normal MCP tool that can create or reveal credentials. The token is displayed once by the administrative command; store it in an approved secret store and supply it only to that one client installation.

Profiles, when the operator elects to use them, remain scope snapshots on the existing V4 agent_clients record. They do not create policy inheritance or allow a later profile edit to widen existing credentials. Project overrides may only narrow a client grant.

Remote MCP configuration contract

Remote clients use the full /mcp endpoint and these runtime references:

AGENT_CONTEXT_MCP_URL=https://agents.example.com/mcp
AGENT_CONTEXT_TOKEN=<dedicated Agent Context credential>

Use bearer authentication:

{
  "Authorization": "Bearer ${AGENT_CONTEXT_TOKEN}"
}

Do not use provider credentials such as GEMINI_API_KEY, GOOGLE_API_KEY, or an Anthropic/OpenAI provider key as Agent Context credentials. Use TLS for all remote deployments. A client-side trust setting or tool filter is never server authorization; the gateway still checks authentication, credential scopes, projects, approval boundaries, revision checks, idempotency, and rate limits.

Local preflight

Run a local, redacting check before configuring a client:

contextctl integration validate gemini-cli

This checks only the local environment-variable shape and TLS//mcp policy. It does not print a token, connect to the endpoint, invoke an MCP tool, or make a paid model call. Use the verification steps printed by contextctl integration show <client> for a deliberate connection test.

Compatibility contract

Before supporting a new client, run the generic compatibility suite. It proves the existing gateway's initialize/connect, tool discovery, bearer authentication, scope/project authorization, reads, writes, project resolution, stable errors, revision conflicts, idempotency, per-client rate limits, and reconnection behavior. The suite uses Codex-like, Claude-like, Gemini-like, and custom fixtures only; it does not require a vendor account or external model call.

Preview and diagnose an evaluation connection

Use the exact origin and project printed/approved during evaluation. Preview is always the default, including when a token path is supplied:

contextctl --json integration doctor codex \
  --origin https://127.0.0.1:YOUR_PORT --project-id evaluation-notes

Replace YOUR_PORT with the actual numeric port. Select claude-code, gemini-cli or custom for their HTTP recipes. The preview returns the existing registry metadata, an actual TOML/JSON fragment and a recipient-terminal command. It opens no active client configuration, token, CA or deployment .env, sends no requests and changes no grants. There is no apply mode. Manually review and merge only the agent-context server into your selected destination, preserving other servers. Replace the stdio launcher/token/CA path placeholders locally.

An explicit live check reads only the selected recipient-owned regular 0600 file and uses this exact origin. A private CA is trusted only for this process:

contextctl --json integration doctor codex \
  --origin https://127.0.0.1:YOUR_PORT --project-id evaluation-notes \
  --token-file /recipient/private/platform-token \
  --ca-file /evaluation/state/tls/ca.crt --connect

Inspect the evaluation CA fingerprint first. Normal public CA trust is used when --ca-file is omitted. Codex's stdio bridge accepts MCP_API_CA_FILE in its process environment for the same scoped trust. For Claude Code/Gemini CLI using a private CA, configure that Node process's reviewed NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS before startup; the doctor does not change vendor client trust. See the official Claude Code CA guidance and Node CA contract. Never bypass certificate validation or silently import an evaluation CA into system trust.

The doctor returns one status/code/next step for each stage:

Stage What it actually proves
Configuration Explicit selection and private credential source are valid; not an audit of installed vendor settings
Transport The selected listener responds; HTTPS certificate/hostname verification passed (loopback HTTP is labeled separately)
Authentication The actual server accepts this credential under current policy
Capabilities Actual MCP initialization, tool discovery and get_platform_capabilities succeed; needs approved agent:self
Project resolve_project resolves the exact selected authorized project; needs projects:read on its directory
Retrieval Project-context search_knowledge succeeds with bounded results; needs coupled search:read and context:read for that project
Policy (requested) --require-read-only checks the server credential's current scopes and coupled tuples contain only reads/agent:self
Write (opt-in) A harmless context probe is created, or an expected read-only refusal is observed, only on the explicit disposable project

A failed stage returns nonzero; later dependent checks remain not_run. Explicit CA inputs must be regular files no larger than 1 MiB; symlinks and devices are refused. Reports contain fixed codes and a result count, never token/header/environment values, private local paths, record IDs or retrieved text. Requests, responses, stdio lifetime and total time are bounded. There is no model-provider call. EMPTY is a successful empty retrieval, not proof of useful knowledge or search relevance. Protocol success is not a claim that an installed vendor CLI was run.

For read-only evaluation, the manager first approves the necessary ceiling and the verified recipient issues a narrower credential without write, approval, promotion, publication, management or session-write scopes. Run doctor with --require-read-only. This verifies server policy; Gemini's existing setup --read-only option remains only a local discovery filter and is labeled as unverified server access. Preview never narrows/replaces an existing credential. Sponsor/team/parent expiry and action/resource grants remain authoritative on every real request. A credential with broader server rights fails the read-only check even if its client hides write tools.

A write check is a separate opt-in:

contextctl --json integration doctor claude-code \
  --origin https://127.0.0.1:YOUR_PORT --project-id evaluation-notes \
  --token-file /recipient/private/platform-token \
  --ca-file /evaluation/state/tls/ca.crt --connect \
  --write-probe --disposable-project-id evaluation-notes

It leaves one clearly labeled context record if allowed. With --require-read-only, only a real gateway write refusal passes this optional check. Do not select a real project as disposable. There is no automatic retry, record deletion, policy update or credential minting. Lost-token replacement continues to require explicit revoke/replacement and new one-time delivery.

The console's Machine clients → View client → Connect this client provides the same offline recipe and staged checklist through its current session-only inspection permission. It never accepts a bearer token or runs a live bearer probe in the browser. The displayed client ceiling and actual credential may differ; terminal doctor verifies the credential separately. Human sessions and machine credentials remain separate.

Client syntax was checked against current official documentation on 27 October 2026: Codex MCP, Claude Code MCP, and Gemini CLI MCP. The existing stdio and Streamable HTTP shapes are preserved. Full release reconciliation remains open.

docs/client-profiles.mdPublic documentation

Public documentation snapshot. Use the generated tool/API reference for contracts in this checkout and live capability discovery for your running deployment.

Client profiles

Client profiles are reusable onboarding templates for the shared MCP gateway. They describe scopes and small operational metadata; each connected client still has its own identity, credential, project grants, and effective authorization. Codex, Claude Code, Gemini CLI, and other MCP clients use the same backend.

Durable model and assignment

client_profiles is a strict, revisioned MongoDB collection. A profile records profile_id, name, description, scopes, optional rate_limit_profile, bounded metadata, and active/disabled status. It stores no token, provider credential, prompt, or arbitrary nested configuration.

agent_clients.profile_id is nullable. Assigning a profile snapshots its scopes onto the client; it does not create policy inheritance. An administrator can supply a strictly narrower scope override and a project override that narrows the client's project grant. Later profile edits do not widen existing clients or already-issued credentials.

Gateway authentication continues to intersect credential, client, scope, and resource grants. rate_limit_profile is descriptive onboarding metadata; the existing per-client gateway settings enforce rate limits.

Recommended templates

The application offers five non-persistent templates. Operators choose whether to save or assign one; startup does not automatically create profiles or clients.

Profile Intended use
coding-agent-default Coding retrieval and context/memory writes
coding-agent-readonly Read-only technical retrieval
research-agent Research acquisition without approval/promotion authority
documentation-agent Documentation retrieval and context/memory updates
creator-agent Planning and drafting without publication authority

coding-agent-default contains skills:read, projects:read, context:read, context:write, memory:read, memory:write, search:read, research:read, research:write, agent:self, session:write, and audit:self:read.

Recommended templates omit agent:manage, research:approve, research:promote, and content:publish. The platform has no broad admin scope; client and credential administration uses the explicit agent:manage capability.

Administrative API

All endpoints require agent:manage; none is a normal agent MCP tool.

Endpoint Purpose
POST /api/v5/client-profiles Create a profile
GET /api/v5/client-profiles Cursor-page profiles
GET /api/v5/client-profiles/{profile_id} Read a profile
PATCH /api/v5/client-profiles/{profile_id} Revision-guarded update
POST /api/v5/client-profiles/{profile_id}/assignments Assign to an existing client

Assignment includes client_id, the client's expected_revision, and optional scope_overrides and project_overrides. Scope overrides must be a subset of the profile scopes. A supplied project list restricts an unrestricted client or narrows an existing allowlist. Concurrent edits return a revision conflict.

Credential and recovery boundaries

A client type such as gemini_cli is provenance/diagnostic metadata. It does not select a different data store or permission implementation. Every installation needs a dedicated Agent Context credential; provider credentials and another client's token are separate.

Migrations 33 and 34 add nullable profile assignment metadata and backfill profile description/status fields without changing existing client grants. Backups cover all collections, including client_profiles. Migration rollback intentionally refuses to remove durable assignment history.

Follow client-onboarding.md for registration and transport configuration, or the Claude Code and Gemini CLI guides for their client settings.

docs/clients/claude-code.mdPublic documentation

Public documentation snapshot. Use the generated tool/API reference for contracts in this checkout and live capability discovery for your running deployment.

Claude Code remote MCP

Managed installation setup

Complete the organization console cutovers first. A lead approves bounded client policy and verified sponsor/team; the authenticated recipient generates their token once. Do not use a legacy operator key recipe to bypass managed issuance. Leads cannot recover another worker's plaintext. Copy explicitly into a private file/approved secret store; retries return metadata and lost delivery needs revoke/replacement. Never store a token in source or browser local/session storage.

Each credential is bound to one organization. Key/client policy intersects current sponsor, team and delegation rights per action/resource in REST and every MCP preflight, including active sessions. Browser cookies cannot authenticate this bearer surface. Provider API keys remain separate. Template edits/disable do not change assigned clients or keys. See managed agents for rotation, expiry, custody, revocation and normal-machine review refusal.

Claude Code and Codex use the same Agent Context MCP server and the same client-neutral tools. Remote clients connect to the Streamable HTTP endpoint:

Claude Code → https://agents.example.com/mcp → Agent Gateway → Context API → MongoDB

There is no Claude-specific endpoint, database, tool, or credential type.

Prerequisites

  • A current Claude Code installation (claude --version).
  • Agent Context deployed at a public or private HTTPS URL ending in /mcp.
  • TLS terminated with a certificate trusted by the Claude Code host. Plain HTTP is appropriate only for a same-machine 127.0.0.1 development deployment.
  • An operator able to administer Agent Context clients and credentials.

Claude Code's current MCP documentation recommends remote HTTP for remote servers. Its documented command is claude mcp add --transport http …; it also supports type: "http" plus environment-variable expansion in the url and headers fields of .mcp.json and user configuration. This guide uses add-json so the shell does not expand or persist a token value.

Create the Claude Code identity and dedicated credential

Run these as an Agent Context operator, substituting the owner and the least privileges required by this client:

contextctl agent create \
  --client-id claude-code-main \
  --type claude_code \
  --name "Claude Code" \
  --owner-id YOUR_OWNER_ID \
  --scope search:read \
  --scope context:read \
  --scope context:write \
  --scope projects:read \
  --scope skills:read \
  --scope memory:read \
  --scope memory:write \
  --scope research:read \
  --scope research:write \
  --scope agent:self \
  --scope session:write \
  --scope audit:self:read

contextctl agent token create claude-code-main \
  --scope search:read \
  --scope context:read \
  --scope context:write \
  --scope projects:read \
  --scope skills:read \
  --scope memory:read \
  --scope memory:write \
  --scope research:read \
  --scope research:write \
  --scope agent:self \
  --scope session:write \
  --scope audit:self:read

The second command displays the generated Agent Context token exactly once. Store it in the operator-approved secret store, then make it available only to the Claude Code process. Do not use, copy, or rename ANTHROPIC_API_KEY or ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN; those authenticate Claude Code to a model provider, not Claude Code to Agent Context.

This is the Claude Code default capability set. It deliberately excludes agent:manage, research:approve, research:promote, and content:publish. Grant any of those only to a separately reviewed client and credential; normal MCP tools never administer credentials.

Set the two dedicated variables in the terminal/session that starts Claude Code. AGENT_CONTEXT_MCP_URL is the full MCP endpoint, not just the origin:

export AGENT_CONTEXT_MCP_URL='https://agents.example.com/mcp'
export AGENT_CONTEXT_TOKEN='paste-the-dedicated-agent-context-token-here'

Never commit either export, a dotenv file containing the token, or an expanded configuration containing the token.

User-scope setup (personal, cross-project)

For personal access across projects, configure the server at Claude Code's user scope. This is the current HTTP remote configuration form, with literal environment references retained by the single quotes:

claude mcp add-json --scope user agent-context \
  '{"type":"http","url":"${AGENT_CONTEXT_MCP_URL}","headers":{"Authorization":"Bearer ${AGENT_CONTEXT_TOKEN}"}}'

This writes a user-scope server definition, not a shell profile. Run it only after exporting the variables for a session where you intend to use it. To inspect the definition and connection status:

claude mcp get agent-context
claude mcp list

Project-scope setup

For a repository-shared server definition, commit the following .mcp.json at the repository root. It intentionally contains variable references, never a credential:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "agent-context": {
      "type": "http",
      "url": "${AGENT_CONTEXT_MCP_URL}",
      "headers": {
        "Authorization": "Bearer ${AGENT_CONTEXT_TOKEN}"
      }
    }
  }
}

Each developer supplies their own AGENT_CONTEXT_TOKEN, issued for their own claude_code client identity. Claude Code asks for approval before using a project MCP server; review the configuration and approve it interactively. Do not bypass that approval. A missing required variable makes Claude Code warn about the configuration; some credential variables may resolve to an empty value. Treat that as a failed setup and fix the process environment — never put a fallback token in .mcp.json.

Verify connection and permissions

Start Claude Code in a shell that has both variables:

claude

Then run /mcp inside Claude Code. agent-context should report as connected. Ask Claude to list the available Agent Context tools, then make these bounded checks:

  1. Ask it to use search_knowledge for a known term.
  2. Ask it to use save_context with an authorized project_id and a harmless test record.
  3. Confirm the saved record through the normal API or search_context.

For a long-running workspace task, Claude Code may call begin_agent_session with the resolved project and a repository label. The shared gateway then correlates subsequent calls such as search_knowledge and save_context in activity and retrieval logs. This lightweight session stores only status, timestamps, project/repository association, and bounded scalar operational metadata; it never stores the Claude conversation, prompt, context window, or private reasoning. End it with end_agent_session using the returned revision when the task finishes.

The available tools are controlled by the credential's scopes and project allowlist. A search:read-only credential can discover and call read tools, but save_context requires context:write; a named project outside the allowlist is refused. The server's configured MCP grant can narrow these permissions further, never widen them.

TLS and deployment

Publish /mcp behind HTTPS in production, normally through the same reverse proxy that exposes the Context API. Keep the API/container network private; the remote edge accepts a bearer credential on every request and forwards it only in process to the existing API authorization path. Do not terminate TLS on an untrusted proxy, disable certificate validation, or put a token in the URL.

Set APP_ENV=production and MCP_REMOTE_ALLOW_LOOPBACK_HTTP=false in a production deployment. If TLS terminates at a reverse proxy, set API_PROXY_HEADERS=true and API_FORWARDED_ALLOW_IPS to that proxy's explicit IP/CIDR allowlist — never *. This lets the server accept the proxy-derived scheme while refusing a public client that merely sends X-Forwarded-Proto. Requests are capped at API_MAX_REQUEST_BYTES; live remote MCP sessions are bounded by MCP_REMOTE_MAX_SESSIONS.

For a local-only development service, http://127.0.0.1:8000/mcp is allowed. It is not a production remote endpoint.

Revocation

Immediately disable the specific Claude Code client if its credential is lost, or revoke the client during offboarding:

contextctl agent revoke claude-code-main

The next MCP tool call is denied, including inside an already-open remote MCP session. Revoking or disabling this client does not affect Codex or any other client's credential.

Rotation

Rotate a Claude credential without interrupting another client: mint a new credential for the same client, update only the Claude Code process's secret store/environment, reconnect and verify search_knowledge, then revoke the old key by its public key ID:

contextctl keys list
contextctl agent token create claude-code-main --scope search:read --scope context:read
contextctl keys revoke --key-id OLD_KEY_ID

Never rotate by reusing a Codex credential or either Anthropic credential. Revocation preserves historical knowledge, content, and actor provenance; it only removes future access.

Troubleshooting

  • UNAUTHENTICATED / HTTP 401: verify that both variables are exported to the process that starts claude, that the URL ends in /mcp, and that the token is the dedicated Agent Context credential.
  • CLIENT_DISABLED / HTTP 403: ask an operator to reactivate or replace the Claude Code client; do not substitute another agent's token.
  • FORBIDDEN or PROJECT_FORBIDDEN: issue only the required scope or add the authorized project to the client's and credential's allowlists.
  • MCP is pending approval: open Claude Code interactively in the project and approve the .mcp.json definition. Inspect it first.
  • TLS failure: fix the server certificate chain or trusted corporate CA; do not disable TLS verification.
  • Configuration parse failure: use "type": "http" with the full endpoint URL. An entry with url but no type is treated as stdio by Claude Code and fails.

Integration-test strategy

CI exercises the MCP SDK's Streamable HTTP client against /mcp, using a dedicated Claude Code client credential. It verifies bearer rejection, revocation, tool discovery, search_knowledge, and save_context, alongside the existing Codex stdio regression surface. It does not invoke a hosted model or real Claude CLI account.

For a manual Claude Code E2E check, configure a user- or project-scope server as above and run scripts/verify-claude-code-mcp.sh with RUN_CLAUDE_CODE_E2E=1 and an authorized test project. The script makes no configuration or shell-profile changes; it only invokes the already configured Claude Code client after explicit opt-in.

Official reference verified

The setup syntax and JSON shape above were verified against Anthropic's current Claude Code MCP documentation, which documents remote HTTP as the recommended transport, --scope user / --scope project, type: "http", bearer headers, ${VAR} expansion, and project MCP approval behavior.

docs/clients/gemini-cli.mdPublic documentation

Public documentation snapshot. Use the generated tool/API reference for contracts in this checkout and live capability discovery for your running deployment.

Gemini CLI remote MCP

Managed installation setup

Complete the organization console cutovers first. A lead approves bounded client policy and verified sponsor/team; the authenticated recipient generates their token once. Do not use a legacy operator key recipe to bypass managed issuance. Leads cannot recover another worker's plaintext. Copy explicitly into a private file/approved secret store; retries return metadata and lost delivery needs revoke/replacement. Never store a token in source or browser local/session storage.

Each credential is bound to one organization. Key/client policy intersects current sponsor, team and delegation rights per action/resource in REST and every MCP preflight, including active sessions. Browser cookies cannot authenticate this bearer surface. Provider API keys remain separate. Template edits/disable do not change assigned clients or keys. See managed agents for rotation, expiry, custody, revocation and normal-machine review refusal.

Gemini CLI connects to the same client-neutral Streamable HTTP endpoint used by Codex and Claude Code:

Gemini CLI → https://agents.example.com/mcp → Agent Gateway → Context API → MongoDB

There is no /mcp/gemini, Gemini-specific server, database, tool, or credential type. Gemini uses the existing /mcp endpoint and its bearer authorization middleware.

Prerequisites

  • A current Gemini CLI installation (gemini --version).
  • Agent Context deployed at a public or private HTTPS URL ending in /mcp.
  • A certificate trusted by the Gemini CLI host. Plain HTTP is only for direct, same-machine 127.0.0.1 development.
  • An Agent Context operator able to create clients and issue credentials.

Use the dedicated Agent Context variables below. Do not substitute GEMINI_API_KEY, GOOGLE_API_KEY, or GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS; those are provider credentials, not Agent Context gateway credentials.

export AGENT_CONTEXT_MCP_URL='https://agents.example.com/mcp'
export AGENT_CONTEXT_TOKEN='<dedicated-agent-context-credential>'

Never commit either export, a dotenv file containing the credential, or a settings file with an expanded credential.

Create gemini-cli-main and a dedicated credential

Run these as an Agent Context operator. Substitute your owner ID and only the projects this client should reach. The client and its credential have separate independent lifecycles from Codex and Claude Code.

contextctl agent create \
  --client-id gemini-cli-main \
  --type gemini_cli \
  --name "Gemini CLI" \
  --owner-id YOUR_OWNER_ID \
  --scope skills:read \
  --scope projects:read \
  --scope context:read \
  --scope context:write \
  --scope memory:read \
  --scope memory:write \
  --scope search:read \
  --scope research:read \
  --scope research:write \
  --scope agent:self \
  --scope session:write \
  --scope audit:self:read

contextctl agent token create gemini-cli-main \
  --scope skills:read \
  --scope projects:read \
  --scope context:read \
  --scope context:write \
  --scope memory:read \
  --scope memory:write \
  --scope search:read \
  --scope research:read \
  --scope research:write \
  --scope agent:self \
  --scope session:write \
  --scope audit:self:read

The credential is shown exactly once. Store it in an approved secret store and make it available only to the Gemini CLI process. The default excludes administrative or high-impact access: admin, agent:manage, credential:manage, research:approve, research:promote, and content:publish are not granted.

Credential lifecycle and log safety

An Agent Context credential is an independently issued acp_… bearer value. The platform persists only its SHA-256 hash, never the plaintext value; the plaintext is returned once at issuance and is never included in gateway responses, activity, audit records, or structured logs. Use an expiry for a workstation credential when operationally appropriate:

contextctl agent token create gemini-cli-main --expires-in-days 90

Rotate by minting a new credential for the same Gemini client, updating only the secret-store injection for that process, reconnecting and verifying it, then revoking the old key by public key ID. Do not copy a Codex or Claude credential into Gemini during rotation. Revocation and expiry are checked on every request, including later calls on an already-open MCP session.

Server alias and transport

Use the stable alias agent-context. Do not use an underscore in an MCP server alias (for example, do not use agent_context): Gemini CLI qualifies tools as mcp_<server>_<tool>, and its policy parser can misidentify aliases that contain underscores. Hyphens are safe.

The examples use httpUrl, which Gemini CLI maps to Streamable HTTP. It must be the complete /mcp endpoint. Do not add url or type alongside it in the same server entry. The current gemini mcp add --transport http command is also supported for managing an HTTP server; its command-managed representation is distinct from this explicit httpUrl settings form.

User-level configuration

Use ~/.gemini/settings.json for personal, cross-project access. Merge this object with other settings already in the file rather than replacing them.

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "agent-context": {
      "httpUrl": "${AGENT_CONTEXT_MCP_URL}",
      "headers": {
        "Authorization": "Bearer ${AGENT_CONTEXT_TOKEN}"
      },
      "timeout": 30000,
      "description": "Agent Context shared MCP gateway",
      "trust": false
    }
  }
}

httpUrl selects the remote Streamable HTTP transport. headers places the dedicated credential in the request's bearer header at runtime, rather than in the file. timeout is milliseconds and description helps identify the connection in Gemini. Keep trust false unless an operator has deliberately reviewed a controlled workflow.

To print the exact token-free fragment without editing a file:

contextctl integration gemini-cli setup --scope user --show-json

The helper only prints configuration and instructions. It does not create a client, issue a credential, edit Gemini settings, set shell variables, or set trust: true.

Project-level configuration

For a repository-specific definition, merge the same token-free fragment into <repository>/.gemini/settings.json:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "agent-context": {
      "httpUrl": "${AGENT_CONTEXT_MCP_URL}",
      "headers": {
        "Authorization": "Bearer ${AGENT_CONTEXT_TOKEN}"
      },
      "timeout": 30000,
      "description": "Agent Context shared MCP gateway",
      "trust": false
    }
  }
}

Every developer supplies an independently issued AGENT_CONTEXT_TOKEN; a repository settings file never carries a shared credential. Print a project-oriented example with:

contextctl integration gemini-cli setup --scope project --show-json

Gemini CLI loads configuration in increasing precedence: built-in defaults, system defaults, user settings, project settings, system settings, environment, then command-line arguments. In particular, a project .gemini/settings.json overrides the user entry for the same setting. Review a repository's settings before running Gemini there, especially if it defines or replaces agent-context.

Before committing a repository, scan the effective .gemini/settings.json and related examples for literal acp_… values. ${AGENT_CONTEXT_TOKEN} is the only credential form appropriate for a tracked settings file.

Tool filtering and read-only discovery

Gemini's includeTools is an allowlist of discovered tools; excludeTools removes tools and takes precedence if a name appears in both lists. They are useful for reducing accidental tool exposure in a particular workspace:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "agent-context": {
      "httpUrl": "${AGENT_CONTEXT_MCP_URL}",
      "headers": {
        "Authorization": "Bearer ${AGENT_CONTEXT_TOKEN}"
      },
      "timeout": 30000,
      "description": "Agent Context shared MCP gateway",
      "includeTools": [
        "get_platform_capabilities",
        "search_knowledge",
        "search_context",
        "search_memory"
      ],
      "excludeTools": ["save_context", "save_memory"],
      "trust": false
    }
  }
}

Use the helper's convenience read-only discovery list when appropriate:

contextctl integration gemini-cli setup --scope project --read-only --show-json

This is not authorization. An includeTools or excludeTools setting changes only what Gemini exposes to its model; removing or editing it cannot grant a gateway action. Issue a credential with read scopes when a client must be read-only. The gateway independently enforces authentication, credential scopes, project access, content-publication approval, research-promotion approval, and expected-revision checks.

Trust guidance

Gemini defaults to trust: false, which retains its normal confirmation behavior. Do not blindly set trust: true: Gemini documents that it bypasses all tool-call confirmations for that server. Even in a deliberately trusted, controlled environment, it does not bypass the Agent Context gateway's authentication, scopes, projects, publication approval, research-promotion approval, or optimistic-concurrency revision checks.

Gateway authorization validation

Gemini's permission decision is made by the existing V4 gateway from the dedicated bearer credential, its linked client, the credential/client scope intersection, and project grants. Gemini's clientInfo, arbitrary HTTP headers, includeTools, excludeTools, and trust setting are not inputs to that decision.

The authorization validation matrix covers three independent credentials: gemini-cli-main, gemini-cli-readonly, and gemini-cli-research. It verifies read-only search and denied writes; permitted context, memory, and research-candidate proposals for the normal/research grants; denied research approval/promotion and content publication without elevated scopes; project denial; and client/scope spoofing attempts. This is shared V4 authorization behavior, not a Gemini exception.

Project resolution, sessions, and provenance

Gemini uses the same V4 resolve_project tool and explicit project_bindings as every other MCP client. Supply one of project_id, git_remote, repository_url, repository_name, or workspace_alias (workspace_hint remains supported for V4 compatibility). Resolution uses only configured exact bindings.
