A result with status: "ambiguous" contains candidates and must be resolved by an explicit operator/client choice; the gateway never guesses a project.

Use begin_agent_session before a related workflow, optionally attaching an authorized project, repository, and small operational metadata such as a workspace label. Use update_agent_session with the returned revision and end_agent_session when work finishes. Session records are operational metadata only; they never persist Gemini conversations, prompts, messages, or transcripts.

Writes made through the gateway are attributed from the dedicated credential, not Gemini settings, clientInfo, caller-provided headers, scopes, or actor claims. For gemini-cli-main, actor provenance is:

{
  "actor_type": "agent",
  "client_id": "gemini-cli-main",
  "client_type": "gemini_cli"
}

The same credential-derived client identity and active session ID correlate gateway activity and retrieval logs for search_knowledge, save_context, save_memory, and authorized research writes. This metadata is diagnostic and auditable; it is not a conversation store. A Gemini credential cannot use another client's session: the gateway checks session ownership against the authenticated client on every session-bound call.

Shared three-agent knowledge workflows

Gemini CLI, Codex, and Claude Code are peers of the same shared platform. An authorized project context or project memory saved by one is discoverable by the others through the same capability-based tools and project grant. There is no per-client context or memory collection.

Operational memory remains isolated: an agent memory belongs only to the credential-linked client, while a project_agent memory belongs only to that client within its explicitly named project. These scopes are derived at the gateway from the bearer identity; no MCP argument can select another client's operational memory.

The shared workflow also retains V4 safety controls. Every durable write has credential-derived actor provenance, guarded updates require the revision a client read, retries with the same Gemini idempotency key create one durable object, and Gemini rate-limit exhaustion does not consume Codex or Claude budgets.

Current gemini mcp management command

The documented Streamable HTTP command syntax is:

gemini mcp add --scope user --transport http \
  --timeout 30000 \
  --description 'Agent Context shared MCP gateway' \
  --header 'Authorization: Bearer ${AGENT_CONTEXT_TOKEN}' \
  agent-context '${AGENT_CONTEXT_MCP_URL}'

Change --scope user to --scope project for project configuration. The current command also supports comma-separated --include-tools and --exclude-tools; use them only as client discovery controls. Omit --trust to retain Gemini's default confirmation behavior. The non-mutating helper prints the matching command for either scope and the read-only option:

contextctl integration gemini-cli setup --scope user
contextctl integration gemini-cli setup --scope project --read-only

Verify the connection

First inspect registration and connection state:

gemini mcp list

Start Gemini CLI with both Agent Context environment variables, then run /mcp list. agent-context should be connected and list discovered tools. Make these bounded checks in order:

  1. Call get_platform_capabilities and confirm gemini-cli-main has the expected non-administrative scopes.
  2. Call search_knowledge for a known term.
  3. Call save_context once with an authorized project_id and harmless test record; review the proposed write.
  4. Confirm the record with search_context or the standard API.

The tools are exactly the same tools Codex and Claude Code use. Project isolation, optimistic concurrency, idempotency, rate limits, provenance, and audit behavior remain unchanged.

TLS, revocation, and troubleshooting

Production remote MCP requires HTTPS. Publish /mcp through a trusted reverse proxy, keep the API/container network private, and never place a bearer token in a URL. Configure API_PROXY_HEADERS=true only together with an explicit API_FORWARDED_ALLOW_IPS proxy IP/CIDR allowlist—never *; an untrusted client-supplied X-Forwarded-Proto cannot upgrade plaintext HTTP. Direct loopback HTTP is development-only. The existing request-size middleware rejects oversized MCP requests before they are read, and the shared gateway applies its bounded fast, standard, and long-running tool timeouts to Gemini exactly as it does to Codex and Claude. If a credential is lost, revoke only its Gemini client:

contextctl agent revoke gemini-cli-main

Codex and Claude Code remain unaffected. Rotate by issuing a new credential, updating Gemini's secret injection, reconnecting and verifying, then revoking the old credential.

  • UNAUTHENTICATED / HTTP 401: verify the Gemini process received both Agent Context variables, the URL ends in /mcp, and the credential is an Agent Context credential.
  • Tools are absent or disconnected: run gemini mcp list, then /mcp list; check whether a higher-precedence project or system setting replaced agent-context.
  • FORBIDDEN or PROJECT_FORBIDDEN: grant only required scopes and projects to both client and credential; do not weaken tool filters or trust.
  • TLS failure: repair the certificate chain or trusted corporate CA; never disable certificate verification.

Official reference verified

The settings paths, precedence, environment interpolation, httpUrl transport, headers, timeout, description, tool filters, alias warning, --scope, and --trust behavior above were checked against Gemini CLI's current MCP server documentation and configuration reference on 2026-10-09.

Codex integration

Managed installation setup

Complete the organization console cutovers first. A lead approves bounded client policy and verified sponsor/team; the authenticated recipient generates their token once. Do not use a legacy operator key recipe to bypass managed issuance. Leads cannot recover another worker's plaintext. Copy explicitly into a private file/approved secret store; retries return metadata and lost delivery needs revoke/replacement. Never store a token in source or browser local/session storage.

Each credential is bound to one organization. Key/client policy intersects current sponsor, team and delegation rights per action/resource in REST and every MCP preflight, including active sessions. Browser cookies cannot authenticate this bearer surface. Provider API keys remain separate. Template edits/disable do not change assigned clients or keys. See managed agents for rotation, expiry, custody, revocation and normal-machine review refusal.

Codex reaches this platform as an MCP server. Nothing about Codex is modified, forked, or patched; it is configured, and it spawns a process that talks to the Context API.

Codex ──stdio/MCP──► MCP server ──HTTP──► Context API ──► services ──► MongoDB

The platform is Codex's durable context layer. Codex keeps its own working context for the session; what is stored here outlives the session, the terminal, and the machine. The two are not connected, and this project never reads or writes Codex's internal state — ~/.codex holds Codex's own databases, and the only file here that belongs to Codex is config.toml.

Configuration

Codex's MCP configuration lives in config.toml: ~/.codex/config.toml for every project, or .codex/config.toml inside a project you have trusted. One table per server, named mcp_servers in snake_case, and command is what selects the stdio transport.

(Syntax verified against the official Codex documentation — see Sources at the end.)

From any project

A project-local .codex/config.toml belongs only to the project where you create it and is not inherited by another repository. If codex mcp get agent-context works here but says the server is absent elsewhere, the user-level entry below is missing.

This is the normal case: some repository you are working in wants the platform. Add to ~/.codex/config.toml, substituting your checkout path:

[mcp_servers.agent-context]
command = "/absolute/path/to/agent-context-platform/scripts/codex-mcp-server.sh"
env = { MCP_API_BASE_URL = "http://127.0.0.1:8000", LOG_LEVEL = "INFO" }
startup_timeout_sec = 30
tool_timeout_sec = 60
required = true

Or let Codex write it:

codex mcp add agent-context \
  --env MCP_API_BASE_URL=http://127.0.0.1:8000 \
  -- /absolute/path/to/agent-context-platform/scripts/codex-mcp-server.sh
codex mcp list

The command must be absolute here, because Codex starts the server from whatever project you are in. The launcher then resolves this repository from its own location, picks .venv/bin/python when one exists, and sets PYTHONPATH — so it works with no virtual environment activated and no inherited PATH.

Inside this repository

The repository ships a token-free opt-in template. Copy it to activate the local configuration:

mkdir -p .codex
cp examples/clients/codex-config.toml .codex/config.toml

Set MCP_API_TOKEN_FILE in the copied file to your dedicated credential path. The template uses a relative launcher command for this checkout; use an absolute launcher path for other repositories. Trust the project when Codex asks. Active .codex/ configuration remains local and is excluded from public releases.

Running the server in a container

If you would rather not run Python on the host:

[mcp_servers.agent-context]
command = "docker"
args = ["compose", "--profile", "mcp", "run", "--rm", "-T", "mcp"]
cwd = "/absolute/path/to/agent-context-platform"
startup_timeout_sec = 60

-T is required: without it Compose allocates a TTY and the protocol stream is corrupted. The container joins the private network and uses MCP_API_BASE_URL=http://context-api:8000, so the host address does not apply. Raise startup_timeout_sec — a container has to be created first.

Configuration keys

Key Purpose Default
command The server to spawn; its presence selects stdio —
args Arguments passed to it []
env Environment variables set for the server —
cwd Working directory to start it from —
startup_timeout_sec How long Codex waits for initialization 10
tool_timeout_sec Per-call timeout 60
enabled Set false to disable without deleting true
required Fail the session if the server cannot start false

Environment variables

These configure the MCP server process, and are set through the env table above. It holds no database credentials: it reaches the platform through the API and nothing else.

Variable Purpose Default
MCP_API_BASE_URL The Context API address http://127.0.0.1:8000
MCP_SERVER_NAME Name Codex shows for the server agent-context-platform
MCP_REQUEST_TIMEOUT_SECONDS Timeout for one API request 30
MCP_SCOPES Comma-separated scopes; empty adds no local narrowing; backend policy still applies empty
MCP_PROJECT_IDS Comma-separated projects; empty adds no local narrowing; backend policy still applies empty
MCP_PROFILE_IDS Comma-separated creator profiles; empty adds no local narrowing; backend policy still applies empty
MCP_API_TOKEN_FILE File holding a bearer token for the API unset
MCP_API_CA_FILE Explicit reviewed private CA for this process; normal hostname verification stays enabled unset (normal public CA trust)
LOG_LEVEL DEBUG…CRITICAL; logs go to stderr INFO

Narrowing is how you hand one Codex session one project:

env = { MCP_API_BASE_URL = "http://127.0.0.1:8000", MCP_PROJECT_IDS = "payment-service", MCP_SCOPES = "search:read,context:read,context:write,memory:read,memory:write" }

That local filter permits only payment-service and eligible organization-global sources; the API still intersects current action/resource and sponsor policy. Local settings alone grant nothing.

For an unmanaged legacy rehearsal only, the historical operator issuance below requires explicit org context and is refused under managed policy. Current managed installations use recipient-only generation described above, then set MCP_API_TOKEN_FILE:

docker compose exec -T context-api python -m app.cli.contextctl --json --org-id YOUR_ORG keys create \
  --name codex-payments \
  --scope search:read --scope context:read --scope context:write \
  --scope memory:read --scope memory:write \
  --project payment-service | jq -r .key > ~/.codex/agent-context-key
chmod 600 ~/.codex/agent-context-key

env = { MCP_API_BASE_URL = "http://127.0.0.1:8000", MCP_API_TOKEN_FILE = "/home/you/.codex/agent-context-key", MCP_PROJECT_IDS = "payment-service" }

A file rather than MCP_API_TOKEN: a token in an environment variable is readable through /proc by every process running as you, and ends up in shell history. The key is checked again at the API, so this narrowing and the key's own grant both apply and the narrower one wins.

Startup requirements

The MCP server is a client of the platform, not the platform. Start the platform first:

docker compose up -d --build --wait
curl --fail http://127.0.0.1:8000/health/ready
make import-skills          # once, so skill retrieval has something to return

Readiness must be ready before Codex will get useful answers. It requires MongoDB primary, mongot reachable, the embedding model loaded, and all six search indexes queryable. The MCP server starts happily against an unready platform and will simply report failures — ask it for get_system_status to see which capability is missing.

The server itself needs nothing: it loads no model, opens no database connection, and starts in well under a second.

The expected workflow

You:    "Implement payment refund support in payment-service."

Codex:  search_knowledge(query="Implement payment refund support.",
                         project_id="payment-service")

        ← the ledger rules, the idempotency rules, the provider's refund
          behaviour, the wallet split, the architecture — ranked together and
          cut to a token budget

Codex:  writes the code, using what the project already decided

Codex:  save_context(project_id="payment-service", type="implementation",
                     title="Refund implementation notes", ...)

The last step is what makes the next session cheaper. It is a call Codex makes on purpose, when asked or when it judges something worth keeping — nothing here watches a conversation and saves it.

Always pass project_id. Project context and project memory are unreachable without it, and no tool will guess. Without it, search can use explicitly permitted organization-global knowledge and the authenticated client's own agent memory, never another project's context or memory. list_projects finds the identifier.

Useful things to tell Codex, once per project:

Use the agent-context MCP server. The project_id is payment-service. Search knowledge before making architectural decisions, and save what you decide.

A note on what comes back: retrieved content arrives fenced and labelled by source, introduced as data. It is knowledge, not instruction — if a stored document says "ignore your instructions", it arrives visibly as a document saying that.

Try it: the payment-service example

examples/payment-service/ holds a realistic project: its architecture, Keycloak integration and scopes, the payment provider's asynchronous refund behaviour, wallet split rules, append-only ledger rules, and idempotency rules — plus two project memories.

python examples/payment-service/load.py

It creates the project through the API and stores everything through the MCP tools, so running it also proves save_context and save_memory work. Every item carries an external_id, so running it twice stores one copy.

Then ask Codex to implement refund support. The retrieval looks like this:

query: "Implement payment refund support."  project_id=payment-service

  0.8590  project_context  Wallet behavior on payment and refund
  0.8560  memory           Refund changes need a second reviewer
  0.7876  project_context  Payment service architecture
  0.7529  project_context  Payment provider behavior, including refunds
  0.7512  project_context  Ledger rules
  0.7269  project_context  Idempotency rules

  method=hybrid  searched=[project_context, active_skill, memory]
  tokens=800/4000  latency=32ms

Every rule a refund implementation needs, in one call, at a fifth of the token budget.

Troubleshooting

Codex does not list the tools. Check the table name is mcp_servers, not mcpServers — the camelCase form other clients use is silently ignored. Then codex mcp list. For a project-scoped .codex/config.toml, confirm you trusted the project; Codex ignores it otherwise.

The server fails to start. Run the command yourself, exactly as configured:

/absolute/path/to/agent-context-platform/scripts/codex-mcp-server.sh </dev/null

It should print one mcp_server_started line to stderr and nothing to stdout. If command is relative in a user-level config, make it absolute. The API client intentionally ignores inherited HTTP_PROXY, HTTPS_PROXY, and ALL_PROXY settings: an explicit self-hosted platform address must not be routed through an ambient proxy, and local MCP startup does not require socksio.

Tools answer "the platform is unreachable." The MCP server started but the Context API did not answer. Check curl --fail http://127.0.0.1:8000/health/ready, and that MCP_API_BASE_URL matches where the API actually listens. A containerised MCP server cannot reach 127.0.0.1 — it needs http://context-api:8000 on the private network.

Searches return nothing. Ask for get_system_status. If a capability is failing, retrieval is degraded rather than broken — lexical search keeps working without the embedding model. If everything is healthy, the content may not be indexed yet: mongot indexes asynchronously, with timing that depends on load and index readiness.

list_skills is empty. Skills are imported, not seeded: run make import-skills.

Everything returns "not authorized". MCP_SCOPES, MCP_PROJECT_IDS, or MCP_PROFILE_IDS may be narrower than the call, or the credential/client may lack the required grant. The message names a missing scope. Correct the intended grant or local restriction; removing a local filter cannot widen the API credential.

A project's context is missing. The call almost certainly omitted project_id, which addresses permitted organization-global/client-operational knowledge, without project-owned records. Nothing infers a project.

The protocol stream is corrupted. Something wrote to stdout. If you wrote a custom launcher, send its diagnostics to stderr; if you are using docker compose run, add -T.

Memory and client boundaries

  • No automatic conversation memory. Memory is written by an explicit save_memory call. Reviewed research candidates have a separate promotion workflow; entire conversations are never converted to memory automatically.
  • No Codex internals. Nothing reads or writes ~/.codex/*.sqlite, and Codex's own context cache is not touched, mirrored, or replaced.

Verification

python -m pytest                                     # includes the shipped configuration
docker compose --profile test run --rm --build test  # live mongod + mongot checks

The configuration itself is under test: that it uses the current table name and the stdio transport, that the command it names exists and is executable, that it carries no credentials, and that the example project validates against the API's own schemas and holds the knowledge the documented refund walkthrough needs.

Public documentation snapshot. Use the generated tool/API reference for contracts in this checkout and live capability discovery for your running deployment.

Content discovery and brief preparation

Content discovery assembles bounded, reviewable inputs for an agent. It does not call an LLM, write an idea automatically, generate body prose, decide novelty, publish anything, or change V1 engineering retrieval.

ContentDiscoveryService reads the existing V1/V2 repositories through profile- and project-bound adapters. Its output is structured data: exact topic labels from stored records, source references, source excerpts, recency data, matching published content, and stored creator/pillar preferences. An agent decides whether to turn that data into prose and must explicitly save any idea.

Discovery

POST /api/v2/content-ideas/discover requires content:read and a creator profile grant. project_id is optional, but project context is inspected only when it is supplied and authorized. Without it, discovery can consider only global memory, trusted active skills, profile-owned published content, and profile pillars; it does not enumerate every V1 project.

{
  "profile_id": "personal-brand",
  "project_id": "payment-service",
  "pillar_id": "payments",
  "platform": "linkedin",
  "time_range": {"start_at": "2026-09-01T00:00:00Z"},
  "limit": 10
}

The response contains candidates with source IDs, related project/pillar, suggested platforms, deterministic usefulness labels, similar published items, and inclusive update-time freshness. It excludes exact-title duplicates among the authorized profile's unpublished ideas and returns those retained ideas so the caller can see why they were not proposed. Time filtering is applied at the repository query and again to every evidence record before candidate assembly.

A project grant is not a relevance grant: a project record becomes a candidate only when it matches the requested pillar, another active pillar, or stored creator interests. This prevents an authorized but unrelated project note from being suggested as content.

Private provenance is never broadened: published records with a project are included only if all their project IDs are the explicit, authorized project. Candidates are separated by source family and project boundary so the displayed IDs can be preserved when an agent elects to save one reviewed idea.

Brief preparation

POST /api/v2/content-briefs/prepare requires content:read. It accepts a saved idea and a destination platform, verifies the profile plus both explicit and idea-origin project grants, and returns a non-persistent brief package: objective, stored audiences, primary message, supporting points, source refs, matched trusted technical skills, one trusted platform-writing skill, similar published records, and constraints derived from stored preferences.

The package always includes do not fabricate project experiences and tells an agent to ground claims in the listed source references. Creator preferences are labels in returned data, not hidden system instructions.

The existing POST /api/v2/content-briefs remains the explicit content:write operation for persisting a reviewed brief. The /prepare route never creates a content_briefs document.

MCP and CLI

The MCP server remains API-only and has no MongoDB credentials:

Tool Scope API
discover_content_ideas content:read POST /api/v2/content-ideas/discover
save_content_idea content:write POST /api/v2/content-ideas
search_content_ideas content:read existing POST /api/v2/content/search with content_ideation and server-side idea kind filtering
prepare_content_brief content:read POST /api/v2/content-briefs/prepare

contextctl content ideas, contextctl content idea create, and contextctl content brief are equally thin API clients. They do not access MongoDB, rank records, or generate content locally.

Persistence and recovery

Discovery uses the existing creator/content collections and full-database backup workflow; it does not persist its preparation results automatically. Startup idempotently reconciles five normal MongoDB recency indexes for active skills, project context, memory scopes, ideas, and published items; these are derived database indexes, not another persistence schema. All source provenance remains in the existing ContentOrigin/ContentSourceReference fields.

docs/content-export.mdPublic documentation

Public documentation snapshot. Use the generated tool/API reference for contracts in this checkout and live capability discovery for your running deployment.

Platform formatting and manual export

Platform adapters format and validate an already stored, agent-authored content item for a supported platform. It does not generate prose, create versions, change lifecycle state, call a remote publishing API, upload a file, or set an external URL. See content-publishing.md for the separate explicit manual-publication receipt.

Platform adapter contract

app.content.platforms.base.ContentPlatform is the small adapter protocol: validate(content), format(content), and export(content, mode). The persisted app.models.content.ContentPlatform enum remains unchanged. The registry currently contains:

Platform Representation Validation and metadata
LinkedIn UTF-8 plain text Normalized readable blank paragraphs and an optional configured character ceiling
Medium Markdown Article title/slug, headings, links, and paired code fences
GitHub Markdown Paired code fences and a suggested README.md, docs/…, or docs/adr/… path

Adapters preserve supplied text apart from stable line endings, trailing whitespace, and the one required document H1 for Markdown representations. They do not make content claims, add engagement language, or connect to any external platform. A deployment may set CONTENT_LINKEDIN_MAX_CHARACTERS to a positive number; leaving it unset imposes no local LinkedIn character ceiling.

API and authorization

POST /api/v2/content/{content_id}/export

The request body has the owning profile_id and a mode of stdout, file, or markdown. It requires content:read, an approved or published item, validates profile access, and checks every project_id and provenance reference before formatting. It returns only a manual export representation: text, format, suggested local names/paths, and platform metadata. file is a client intent, not permission for the API server to write a file.

No response performs an external request or changes status, published_at, external_url, current_version, or provenance.

CLI

# print an API-returned representation
contextctl content export --profile-id personal-brand --content-id retry-post --mode stdout

# ask for Markdown formatting and print it
contextctl content export --profile-id personal-brand --content-id architecture-article --mode markdown

# opt in to a local UTF-8 write; existing files need an explicit --force
contextctl content export --profile-id personal-brand --content-id readme-draft \
  --mode file --output ./README.md

The CLI always calls the protected API for authorization and formatting. Only its explicit --mode file --output PATH writes locally; it creates missing parent directories and refuses to overwrite an existing file without --force. It never uses suggested paths automatically and never publishes.

Persistence and operations

Export adds no collection, index, migration, backup input, search index, embedding, or MCP tool. It formats the current stored item only, so immutable content versions remain untouched and embeddings continue to use the existing current-representation policy.

docs/content-metrics.mdPublic documentation

Public documentation snapshot. Use the generated tool/API reference for contracts in this checkout and live capability discovery for your running deployment.

Content metrics

The metrics workflow stores content performance observations as generic, append-only data in the existing MongoDB content_metrics collection. It does not depend on an analytics provider: the supported workflow is an explicit manual capture.

What one observation contains

Every observation is owned by a creator profile and one existing content item:

  • metric_id is unique within the profile and deterministically derives the BSON _id.
  • content_id and platform identify the observed representation.
  • captured_at is the time the values were observed.
  • metrics is a non-empty map of non-negative finite numeric values.
  • source defaults to manual; it records provenance only and never triggers a provider call.
  • provider_metadata is optional descriptive metadata; it does not invoke an integration.
  • Standard timestamps, a revision, tags, and an active/archived lifecycle field are retained.

Common metric names are views, impressions, likes, comments, shares, clicks, bookmarks, and followers_gained. They are not an exhaustive vocabulary. Generic keys let a provider expose a useful, reviewed measurement without a schema rewrite.

The API rejects empty maps, invalid metric names, boolean values, negative numbers, infinities, and NaN. It also rejects a duplicate profile/metric ID. Metrics are immutable observations: correcting a value means recording a new capture with a new ID, not overwriting history.

API and access controls

POST /api/v2/content/{content_id}/metrics requires content:write. GET /api/v2/content/{content_id}/metrics and the get_content_metrics MCP tool require content:read.

Both routes require access to the profile and, before returning or writing any metric, to every project referenced by the content item. The list endpoint supports platform, captured_after, captured_before, limit, and an opaque cursor; captures are ordered newest-first by captured_at.

The metrics service has no analytics client and does not mutate creator profiles, voice, content pillars, or content. It produces no strategy insight or engagement optimization. Any later insight feature must be an explicitly reviewed, advisory layer.

Persistence and recovery

Migration 12 adds source and provider_metadata to the already-existing content_metrics collection. It first loosens only those required fields, backfills legacy captures as source: "manual" with empty metadata, then restores strict validation. It is idempotent and does not modify any V1 collection.

The existing backup workflow uses mongodump for the entire application database and records per-collection counts in its manifest. Therefore it already includes content_metrics and continues to restore it without a separate content database or backup rule. Standard MongoDB indexes include the profile/content/platform/captured-at time-series query path.

docs/content-planning.mdPublic documentation

Public documentation snapshot. Use the generated tool/API reference for contracts in this checkout and live capability discovery for your running deployment.

Novelty checks and repurposing plans

The planning services provide planning evidence around content that already exists. It does not call an LLM, generate a draft, create a version, publish anything, or declare that a topic is objectively novel. Creator content and retrieved text remain data, not instructions.

Advisory novelty checks

POST /api/v2/content/novelty requires content:read, a profile grant, and a project grant when project_id is supplied. It searches the existing content history through the content_history retrieval profile, then compares normalized title/tag/pillar terms (topic) and descriptive terms (angle).

{
  "profile_id": "personal-brand",
  "title": "Monitoring Outbox delivery lag",
  "description": "Explain alerting on lag and exhausted retries rather than implementation.",
  "tags": ["outbox", "payments"],
  "project_id": "payment-service",
  "method": "hybrid",
  "limit": 10
}

The result is explicitly advisory: true. Its classifications are same-topic-same-angle, same-topic-new-angle, related-topic, and new-topic; they are stable planning labels, not truth claims. Each visible match retains its identifier, kind, platform/status, source references, shared terms, and topic/angle overlap. A history record that references a project the caller cannot access is discarded before comparison, so its scores and existence cannot leak.

Repurpose plans

POST /api/v2/content/{id}/repurpose takes a profile, targets, and an optional source_kind (content, brief, or idea; content is the default). It first loads and authorizes that stored source, then returns a read-only plan. It accepts LinkedIn, Medium, and GitHub targets today; adding a platform is localized to ContentPlatform and its structural planning metadata.

The plan contains a core thesis, bounded source excerpts, explicit source provenance, examples that are present in the source, target-specific fields to shorten or expand, structural destination differences, the reviewed canonical platform-writing skill, and visible related history. It contains no target body, no generated draft, and no persistence operation. A one-sentence source is deliberately represented by a stable evidence label rather than returned verbatim as a purported plan.

The content skill selection is trusted-active-only. Its canonical Git-backed Markdown file remains the writing guidance; platform metadata in the service only describes output structure and does not generate prose.

MCP and CLI

The thin MCP server calls the same API routes only:

Tool Scope API
check_content_novelty content:read POST /api/v2/content/novelty
prepare_repurpose_plan content:read POST /api/v2/content/{id}/repurpose

contextctl content novelty and contextctl content repurpose are equally thin API clients. Neither reads MongoDB, computes an overlap, generates a draft, nor writes content locally.

Persistence and recovery

Novelty and repurposing results are read-only planning data. It reuses content_ideas, content_briefs, content_items, and the existing retrieval/backup/restore path. Saving a resulting idea or draft is a separate, explicit write operation.

docs/content-publication-safety.mdPublic documentation

Public documentation snapshot. Use the generated tool/API reference for contracts in this checkout and live capability discovery for your running deployment.

Publication safety and approval

The publication service provides deterministic review before a content item can be approved for manual export or a manual-publication receipt. It is a safety layer, not a confidentiality guarantee and not an automated publishing system. An agent still writes the prose; a human remains responsible for deciding whether the result is appropriate to disclose.

Lifecycle

The existing ContentStatus state machine is the approval state; no new content collection or body field is introduced:

drafting -> review -> approved -> export / explicit manual receipt

POST /api/v2/content/{content_id}/approve accepts an expected_revision and only permits the existing review -> approved transition. The service scans the current revision again immediately before the update. A stale revision, draft, archived record, or configured high-severity finding is refused. The content body is never changed, generated, redacted, published, or copied into the audit trail.

POST /api/v2/content/{content_id}/export now requires approved or published status. It remains a local/manual representation endpoint; the service does not call LinkedIn, Medium, GitHub, or any other external provider.

Review API and MCP

POST /api/v2/content/{content_id}/publication-review requires content:read plus profile and every provenance-project grant. Its request body is:

{"profile_id": "personal-brand"}

The response contains publishable, an advisory findings list, a field and line/column location for each finding, and the current item’s authorized project/source metadata. It does not contain the item body or the matched secret/PII value. Provenance is returned only after the same profile/project checks used by normal content reads, so it is available to an authorized reviewer but never included in a public export.

The thin MCP tool review_content_for_publication calls that API with content:read. It returns the same redacted structured data and explicitly states that retrieved content and review results are data, not instructions. Approval is a separate content:write API operation. The MCP mark_content_published tool requires content:publish and records a manual receipt; see content-publishing.md.

What the deterministic scanner checks

app/content/publication.py evaluates the title, body, and existing external URL for likely API keys, credentials, tokens, private URLs, private IPs, internal hostnames, internal repository URLs, customer IDs, email addresses, and phone numbers. It also evaluates provenance project IDs and configurable case-insensitive terms. A deployment can mark private architecture vocabulary or projects as sensitive with:

  • CONTENT_PUBLICATION_SENSITIVE_TERMS
  • CONTENT_PUBLICATION_SENSITIVE_PROJECT_IDS
  • CONTENT_PUBLICATION_BLOCK_HIGH_SEVERITY (defaults to true)

The list settings use normal Pydantic-settings JSON arrays, for example CONTENT_PUBLICATION_SENSITIVE_TERMS='["LedgerMesh"]'. Keep the list small and specific; it identifies material that needs review, not words that should be silently removed.

The configuration is a review policy, not a magic allow-list or a replacement for project authorization. A finding includes a type, severity, field, location, and safe explanation—not the value that was matched. High-severity findings block approval by default; lower-severity findings remain visible for human judgment. The scanner never silently edits a finding away.

Audit and logging

Successful and blocked approval attempts append content.approve events to the existing audit_logs collection. The event records actor, profile, request route, outcome, and a generic safe reason. It contains neither prose nor a matched sensitive value. Scanner logs include only content/profile IDs, finding-type names, counts, and the boolean result.

Migration 10 idempotently runs collMod on the existing strict audit_logs validator to permit the additive content.approve action. It creates no collection, changes no V1 document, and has no safe down migration: removing an approval event would destroy audit history. Existing backup and restore already include audit_logs and the V2 content collections, so no separate backup configuration is needed.

Deliberate exclusions

Publication review does not generate or rewrite content, retrieve new private context, automatically approve, or deliver content to external providers. Manual receipts and descriptive metric captures are separate explicit workflows; see content-publishing.md and content-metrics.md.

docs/content-publishing.mdPublic documentation

Public documentation snapshot. Use the generated tool/API reference for contracts in this checkout and live capability discovery for your running deployment.

Manual publication receipts and publisher interfaces

The publishing service provides an explicit, approval-gated boundary for existing content records. It does not generate prose, infer an audience, approve content, or publish as a side effect of creation, editing, versioning, retrieval, export, or MCP discovery.

Default deployment

The default and only enabled provider is ManualPublisher. It has no credentials, makes no network call, and records a human-confirmed publication of an already-approved stored item. A human may export the item, complete the platform action outside this service, and then explicitly mark that exact item published.

github, linkedin, and medium are durable provider vocabulary only. They are not adapters, are not configured, and return a safe "not configured" failure. The platform therefore continues to work normally when all external adapters are disabled.

Safety and lifecycle

The only supported transition into published is:

drafting -> review -> approved -> explicit publish

The publish service reloads the current item, checks its optimistic revision, requires approved, and runs the deterministic safety review again. Configured blocking findings stop the action. This remains a safety layer, not a guarantee of confidentiality.

Generic content updates cannot set published, published_at, provider, external ID, external URL, or the publication idempotency key. Creating a new version returns the new current item to drafting and clears its current publication receipt. Immutable content versions and audit records remain unchanged.

API and MCP

POST /api/v2/content/{content_id}/publish requires content:publish, profile access, every referenced project grant, and:

{
  "profile_id": "personal-brand",
  "expected_revision": 4,
  "provider": "manual",
  "idempotency_key": "manual-publish-2026-09-24"
}

It deliberately accepts no body, title, destination path, provider credential, or arbitrary text. The response contains the persisted current item and the redacted provider receipt: provider, optional external ID/URL, timestamp, and idempotency key.

The thin MCP tool mark_content_published forwards those same fields to the API. It cannot query MongoDB directly and it cannot publish arbitrary text.

Every attempt is auditable as content.publish with allowed, denied, or failed outcome. Audit reasons are fixed classifications, not provider error payloads or content. Provider failures are returned as a generic error and logs never include provider credentials or provider response bodies.

Idempotency and retries

If no key is supplied, the service uses the deterministic key publish:{content_id}:{current_version}. ManualPublisher supports idempotency. Retrying a completed action with the same provider and key returns the stored receipt without calling the provider again. A different key for the same current published representation is refused.

A provider must declare idempotency support before this service will use it. If a concurrent persistence update loses the optimistic race, the service re-reads the item and returns the existing matching receipt; otherwise it asks the caller to re-read and retry. This prevents a retry from silently delivering a second publication.

Persistence and migration

Migration 11 adds nullable fields to the existing V2 content_items collection:

  • publication_provider
  • external_id
  • publication_idempotency_key

It first applies a temporary strict validator that permits the new properties, backfills each missing field with null, then restores the final strict validator. It also permits the additive content.publish action on the existing audit_logs validator. The migration is idempotent and irreversible: deleting an auditable publication receipt or decision would lose history.

No collection, index, database, vector store, embedding, or backup target is added by publication receipts. Full-database backup and restore procedures include content_items and audit_logs.

Adding an external adapter later

An external adapter must implement Publisher in app/content/publishers/base.py: publish, validate_connection, and get_publication_status. It must be explicitly registered, use a scoped credential source, redact errors, honor the supplied idempotency key, and remain disabled unless configured. A future GitHub adapter must use a repository-scoped, least-privilege token; organization-wide or unrestricted repository access is not acceptable.

Deliberate exclusions

The release contains no GitHub, LinkedIn, or Medium network adapter, no credential settings, no direct external publishing by default, no background publication, no automatic approval, and no external analytics collection. Explicit manual metric observations are documented in content-metrics.md.

docs/content-retrieval.mdPublic documentation

Public documentation snapshot. Use the generated tool/API reference for contracts in this checkout and live capability discovery for your running deployment.

Content retrieval

Content retrieval makes the current representations in content_ideas, content_briefs, and content_items searchable. It reuses the existing local embedding provider, MongoDB Search, MongoDB Vector Search/mongot, and the pure hybrid-ranking primitive. It does not alter V1 engineering retrieval, generate prose, discover ideas, repurpose content, or publish anything.

What is indexed

Migration 9 adds nullable embedding metadata to ideas, briefs, and current content items: embedding, embedding_model, embedding_dimensions, and embedding_generated_at. It first backfills null values and then reconciles the strict validators, making it safe to apply to a populated development database. content_versions is deliberately unchanged: version history stays append-only and is never turned into a duplicate vector corpus.

The content service embeds the current idea and brief representation on write. It embeds an item only while its current status is drafting, approved, or published; a transition to a non-meaningful current representation removes that item's stale vector. An archived item remains lexically searchable. Body changes create a new immutable version and re-embed only the new current copy.

Startup reconciles six derived indexes idempotently:

Collection Lexical index Vector index
content_ideas content_idea_text_index content_idea_vector_index
content_briefs content_brief_text_index content_brief_vector_index
content_items content_item_text_index content_item_vector_index

Every index has profile_id as a pre-filter. The applicable platform, project, status, pillar, and tag fields are also filters, so MongoDB restricts the candidate set before scoring rather than leaking or losing recall after search. Normal MongoDB embedding-model indexes support later re-embedding work.

API and authorization

POST /api/v2/content/search requires content:read and an explicit profile_id.

{
  "profile_id": "personal-brand",
  "query": "What have I written about idempotency?",
  "kinds": ["content"],
  "retrieval_profile": "content_history",
  "method": "hybrid",
  "platform": "linkedin",
  "project_id": "payments-api",
  "status": "published",
  "pillar_id": "payments",
  "tags": ["idempotency"],
  "token_budget": 1200,
  "limit": 10
}

method is lexical, vector, or hybrid; hybrid is the default. Optional kinds is a unique subset of idea, brief, and content; omitting it keeps the existing all-current-representations search. The response includes the result type, current text, score, methods, token count, and retained provenance (project_ids and source_refs). The caller needs a profile grant and, where supplied, the requested project grant. A broad search also silently removes any result whose recorded project provenance is not allowed by the caller's project grant. This avoids confirming that private project-derived material exists.

GET /api/v2/content/{content_id}/versions?profile_id=… is a read-only, cursor-paginated history endpoint used by the MCP history tool. It applies the same profile and current-item provenance checks before returning snapshots.

Retrieval profiles

The V2-only profiles are content_creation, content_history, content_ideation, and content_repurposing. They use separate content ranking weights, so tuning them does not change V1 engineering ranking.

The configurable initial content_creation priorities are:

Source Default
project_context 1.00
memory 0.95
technical_skill 0.85
content_skill 0.85
published_content 0.70
conversation 0.40

They are exposed through CONTENT_CREATION_PRIORITY_* settings. The content search endpoint searches only content collections. Cross-source discovery and brief preparation use their own explicit workflows; these priorities do not widen this endpoint or change engineering search. See content-discovery.md.

MCP

The thin, read-only MCP tools call the API only:

Tool Scope API
search_content content:read POST /api/v2/content/search
get_content content:read GET /api/v2/content/{id}
get_content_history content:read GET /api/v2/content/{id}/versions

Their prompt-facing renderings fence every retrieved body and label it as data, not instructions. MCP holds no MongoDB credential, repository, vector query, or ranking logic.

Recovery

The new vectors stay in the existing MongoDB collections. Existing complete database backup, restore, and manifest-count verification therefore include them automatically; no content database or vector store is introduced.

docs/content-schema.mdPublic documentation

Public documentation snapshot. Use the generated tool/API reference for contracts in this checkout and live capability discovery for your running deployment.

Creator and content schema

The creator/content system stores structured preferences, ideas, briefs, drafts, versions, provenance, and metrics. See creator.md for profile/pillar interfaces, content-storage.md for lifecycle APIs, and content-retrieval.md for current-content retrieval. It has no content generation or autonomous strategy analysis; metrics remain descriptive data only. Content agents remain responsible for writing prose; this platform stores structured data, provenance, revisions, and lifecycle state.

Collections

Collection Profile ownership Purpose
creator_profiles profile_id Communication preferences as data, never hidden instructions
content_pillars profile_id Long-lived themes and priority
content_ideas profile_id Candidate topics and initial origin
content_briefs profile_id Platform-specific evidence plan
content_items profile_id Current working copy of a content item
content_versions profile_id Append-only snapshots for a content item
content_links profile_id Provenance relations to source knowledge
content_metrics profile_id Timestamped, generic metric observations
content_campaigns profile_id Coordinated sets of related content

All records carry an _id, UTC created_at and updated_at timestamps, and a positive revision. The named record types use deterministic BSON ObjectIds from their profile and public IDs; versions additionally include (content_id, version). MongoDB strict validators and normal indexes mirror the Pydantic models. Standard index initialization is idempotent. Derived content Search and Vector Search indexes are described in content-retrieval.md.

Content repositories are bound to exactly one profile for every read, list, write, and revision-guarded update. A caller cannot use a profile-scoped repository to read or mutate a different profile's data. content_versions and content_metrics intentionally expose append-and-list storage only, preserving history rather than enabling accidental overwrites.

Vocabulary and provenance

The shared content lifecycle values are idea, selected, researching, brief_ready, drafting, review, approved, published, and archived. The supported platform enum contains linkedin, medium, and github; adding a future destination such as YouTube, X, Reddit, a newsletter, or a blog is localized to the platform enum and MongoDB validator rather than platform branches in storage code.

content_links accepts derived_from, mentions, explains, documents, updates, and contrasts. Briefs and content items also record source references with source_type, source_id, and optional project_id. That keeps project context identifiable as data. The publication review service uses this provenance when assessing a stored draft; provenance alone is not permission to publish.

Migration and recovery

Migration 6 creates or reconciles these nine strict collections and their validators. It is additive: no V1 collection is renamed or structurally changed. Its rollback is deliberately refused because dropping content history or provenance would lose authored records.

Migration 7 adds an empty-default tone_preferences field to creator profiles, an empty-default profile allow-list to API keys, and an optional profile target in audit records. It safely backfills only those defaults before reconciling the affected strict validators. An empty key allow-list preserves the V1 meaning of access to every profile for that historical schema. V6 adoption records it as explicit all_in_org in the selected organization; new managed NONE policy is distinct and never serialized as an empty legacy ALL array.

Backups already dump the complete configured MongoDB database and record a collection-count manifest. Consequently the new collections are included in new backups and verified restores automatically; no separate content database or backup path exists. Managed restore verification compares each collection count and required metadata, including these V2 collections, in isolated temporary storage. A combined count alone cannot establish preservation.

Migration 12 backfills the existing content_metrics collection with a source (default manual) and an empty provider_metadata object, then restores strict validation. Captures remain append-only and use the existing profile/content/platform/captured-at index; it adds no collection, external analytics dependency, or V1 change. The API and MCP boundary are documented in content-metrics.md.

Creator/profile routes use creator:read and creator:write; content storage uses content:read and content:write. Publication requires the separate content:publish scope. Allowed content mutations record content.write audit events. Migration 8 adds that action to the existing strict audit validator; no V1 route or document structure changes. Migration 9 adds nullable embedding metadata only to current ideas, briefs, and content items, preserving immutable content_versions; its derived Mongo Search/Vector Search indexes and current representation policy are documented in content-retrieval.md. Existing V1 routes and their authorization behavior remain unchanged.

Research-backed content briefs and fact review

Research evidence can be linked into the existing content_briefs collection. A brief may retain a research_project_id, frozen claim_refs, frozen citation_refs (including source class, excerpt, source snapshot, and locator), and factual_review_status.

factual_review_status is one of not_reviewed, verified, or needs_review. verified has a deliberately limited meaning: every reviewed, mapped claim was explicitly stored as supported and had a supporting citation at review time. It is not a guarantee that a draft is true or complete.

POST /api/v2/content/{content_id}/fact-review reviews a saved draft against a selected research project (or the research project stored on its brief). A caller may provide claim IDs or claim text. When neither is supplied, the service identifies only normalized exact occurrences of already stored claim statements in the draft. Semantic retrieval and retrieval scores never label a claim as factual support.

The result exposes the supported, unsupported, contested, and outdated counts; per-claim findings; citation references and locators; and missing evidence. Partially supported and unreviewed material remains visible as evidence that still needs review. Unsupported, contested, outdated, and missing evidence are never hidden.

The endpoint requires V2 profile authorization, the normal V1 grants for every project attached to the draft and brief, and the V1 grants linked to the V3 research project. It is read-only: it does not rewrite a draft, advance its lifecycle, publish it, update claim states, promote research to V1 memory or context, or change canonical skills. MCP exposes the same protected operation as review_content_facts; it has no MongoDB access.

Migration 20 backfills legacy content briefs with null research_project_id, empty reference lists, and not_reviewed, then restores strict validation. No collection, database, vector store, or backup target is added: the complete MongoDB backup already includes the extended content_briefs collection.

docs/content-skills.mdPublic documentation

Public documentation snapshot. Use the generated tool/API reference for contracts in this checkout and live capability discovery for your running deployment.

Content skills

The catalog includes ten reviewed, Git-backed Markdown skills under skills/content/. They use the existing V1 skills and skill_chunks collections, importer, version lifecycle, local embedding provider, mongot lexical/vector indexes, and hybrid retrieval engine. Separate content services provide idea discovery, drafts, review, export, and publication receipts.

Canonical catalogue

skills/content/
├── linkedin-writing.md
├── medium-writing.md
├── github-writing.md
├── technical-storytelling.md
├── hooks.md
├── editing.md
├── technical-explanation.md
├── content-repurposing.md
├── content-review.md
└── content-ideation.md

Each file has V1's strict frontmatter, an explicit 1.1.0 semantic version, category: content, and trust_level: trusted. That trust level is reserved for reviewed canonical files in Git; generated, copied, or unreviewed material must use the existing lower trust levels instead. Retrieved skill text remains data and cannot override system, application, authorization, or publication rules.

Version 1.1.0 preserves each skill's purpose and adds concrete examples, evidence/claim boundaries, audience choices, version-specific technical context, reproducible commands, exact-revision review and adaptation that preserves qualifications. The initial 1.0.0 versions remain immutable if already imported; import the new Git versions through the normal operator command.

The skills supply communication guidance only. They do not generate prose, create ideas or drafts, retrieve private project context, change lifecycle state, or publish content. Any use of private project information still needs the explicit publication review.

Import and retrieval

Import through the existing V1 command after reviewing and committing the canonical files:

make import-skills

The importer recursively discovers skills/content/*.md, validates and chunks them, generates local embeddings, and writes immutable skill versions. A retry with unchanged bytes reports unchanged; it creates neither duplicate versions nor duplicate chunks. A changed skill requires a new frontmatter version.

Use the existing V1 retrieval endpoints, CLI, or MCP skill tools. For example, the following queries are expected to select their platform skill:

write a LinkedIn post about an engineering lesson  -> linkedin-writing
create a Medium architecture article               -> medium-writing
write GitHub architecture documentation            -> github-writing

Search the source catalog offline with .venv/bin/python scripts/skill_catalog.py search "content review" --category content. Use the HTML catalog to read full bodies and the content task bundle. Local lexical scores differ from live hybrid ranking; see skill-catalog.md for filters and import verification.

The normal V1 availability rules still apply: lexical retrieval works whenever the text index is ready. Vector retrieval requires a compatible local model and ready vector index; hybrid retrieval can fall back to lexical results when embedding is unavailable, with that degradation reported in retrieval metadata. See skills.md, embeddings.md, and retrieval.md for the shared mechanics.

Safety emphasis

The platform does not treat these files as hidden system instructions. Their guidance explicitly rejects fabricated stories, unsupported achievements, engagement bait, accidental disclosure of private project context, and automatic publication. Content review is always an explicit human action.

docs/content-storage.mdPublic documentation

Public documentation snapshot. Use the generated tool/API reference for contracts in this checkout and live capability discovery for your running deployment.

Content storage and lifecycle

The content storage API keeps manually supplied ideas, briefs, drafts, immutable versions, and provenance under profile and project grants. Agents write the content; the platform stores and validates it. Dedicated retrieval, planning, review, export, and publication workflows build on this storage layer.

REST API

Every storage endpoint below is under /api/v2, requires a content:read or content:write scope, and takes an explicit profile_id in its query or request body. The profile must be allowed by the API key. Any project named by an origin, source reference, or content project_ids also needs the key's project grant before it is returned or stored.

Method Path Scope Purpose
GET /content-ideas?profile_id=… content:read Cursor-page a profile's ideas
POST /content-ideas content:write Create an initial idea
PATCH /content-ideas/{idea_id} content:write Revision-guard idea metadata or lifecycle
POST /content-briefs content:write Store an evidence-backed brief
GET /content-briefs/{brief_id}?profile_id=… content:read Read one authorized brief
POST /content content:write Create a draft plus immutable version 1
GET /content/{content_id}?profile_id=… content:read Read one item, including archived items
PATCH /content/{content_id} content:write Revision-guard metadata/lifecycle, never the body
POST /content/{content_id}/versions content:write Append a body or rollback as a new version
GET /content/{content_id}/versions?profile_id=… content:read Cursor-page immutable history after provenance checks
POST /content/search content:read Search current content representations
POST /content/{content_id}/export content:read Validate and return a manual representation without state change

The idea list uses the platform's opaque created_at/_id cursor and limits from 1 to 50. Repository-level content and version listing likewise retains archived records. Retrieval covers current ideas, briefs, and items; its API, indexes, privacy behavior, and MCP tools are documented in content-retrieval.md.

Lifecycle and immutable versions

New ideas start at idea; new content items always start at drafting. The lifecycle progresses through selected, researching, brief_ready, drafting, review, approved, published, and archived. Approval uses the dedicated review/approval operation; publication uses the separate content:publish receipt operation. A normal PATCH cannot bypass these steps. See publication safety and manual publishing. A transition from published to drafting is rejected by a normal PATCH. An explicit version request is the revision workflow: it creates a new draft snapshot while keeping the previously published snapshot unchanged.

Content bodies cannot appear in PATCH /content/{id}. Creating a content item writes content_items and content_versions version 1 in one MongoDB transaction. A later version request writes the next immutable snapshot and updates the current copy in the same transaction, using the item's expected_revision. A stale request returns a conflict rather than creating a partial history entry.

To roll back, send rollback_to_version instead of body to the version endpoint along with expected_revision, change_reason, and optionally created_by. The platform copies the historical body into a new latest version. It never edits or deletes the earlier version.

source_refs, project_ids, tags, and source links remain explicit data. They are not instructions and are not included automatically in exported prose. content_links and content_campaigns have profile-isolated service support for manually supplied provenance and grouping data; their public REST workflows remain internal service operations because the public REST contract does not define link or campaign endpoints.

Export formats an authorized current item for manual use, but does not write a version, alter its lifecycle, set a public URL, or publish it. Its platform-specific representations are described in content-export.md.

Audit and migration

Allowed mutations record the content.write audit action with the profile ID, HTTP method, and route, never the content body. Migration 8 widens only the existing strict audit_logs validator to accept that additive action. It does not alter V1 documents or any V2 content document shape. Existing V2 content collections, indexes, and backup/restore coverage remain those created by Migration 6.

docs/creator.mdPublic documentation

Public documentation snapshot. Use the generated tool/API reference for contracts in this checkout and live capability discovery for your running deployment.

Creator profiles and content pillars

Creator profiles store communication preferences, while content pillars group themes within a profile. The API supports profile/pillar CRUD, profile-scoped authorization, thin MCP tools, and API-backed contextctl commands. See content-skills.md for writing guidance, content-storage.md for drafts and versions, and content-discovery.md for planning.

Preference data, never hidden instructions

A creator profile is structured data about how its owner prefers to communicate. It may contain audiences, domains, structured voice tone/avoidance values, writing, formatting, terminology, language, and tone preferences, topics of interest or avoidance, and content objectives. It has no prompt or executable instruction field. MCP labels every returned profile as retrieved data, not instructions.

Profiles have active, inactive, or archived status. Inactive and archived profiles remain readable to an authorized caller. Profiles do not generate prose; the calling agent interprets them as preference data.

Pillars are profile-owned, revisioned themes. A pillar has an identifier, name, description, tags, 0..1 priority, and active/archived status. A pillar cannot be created or updated outside its explicit profile_id boundary.

API

All endpoints are under /api/v2 and use the existing bearer-key authentication.

Method Path Scope Notes
GET /creator-profiles creator:read Cursor-paginated; only granted profiles appear.
POST /creator-profiles creator:write Creates a deterministic profile_id.
GET /creator-profiles/{profile_id} creator:read Requires an explicit profile grant.
PATCH /creator-profiles/{profile_id} creator:write Requires expected_revision.
GET /content-pillars?profile_id=… creator:read Cursor-paginated inside exactly one profile.
POST /content-pillars creator:write Profile must already exist.
PATCH /content-pillars/{pillar_id} creator:write Body contains profile_id and expected_revision.

PATCH operations are optimistic: a stale expected_revision returns 409 rather than overwriting a concurrent change. The API never accepts a project_id for these resources, so V1 project context cannot be implicitly attached or disclosed through these endpoints.

Profile grants

creator:read and creator:write authorize the resource type. An API key can also be narrowed to creator profiles with repeatable --profile:

contextctl keys create --name personal-brand-agent \
  --scope creator:read --scope creator:write \
  --profile personal-brand

Omitting --profile retains the established V1 convention of an unrestricted grant. A restricted key receives neither a profile listing entry nor a successful lookup for an ungranted profile. The same scope names also include separate content:read and content:write grants for briefs, drafts, and content items.

MCP has an independent, optional MCP_PROFILE_IDS allow-list. It is checked before an MCP request reaches the API, then the API key is checked again. The narrower of the two grants wins.

MCP tools

Tool Scope Operation
get_creator_profile creator:read Read one profile as data.
update_creator_profile creator:write Revision-guarded partial update.
list_content_pillars creator:read Page pillars in one explicit profile.

The MCP server remains a thin HTTP client. It does not connect to MongoDB, make lifecycle decisions, or turn profile preferences into instructions.

CLI

The commands call the V2 API; they do not duplicate service or MongoDB logic.

contextctl creator show --profile-id personal-brand
contextctl creator update --profile-id personal-brand --expected-revision 3 \
  --status inactive --audience "software architects"
contextctl creator pillars --profile-id personal-brand --limit 20

creator update sends only named changes. Supplying the structured voice fields requires both --voice-tone and --voice-avoid, preventing an accidental replacement of half the voice object.

Migration and verification

Migration 7 backfills empty tone_preferences on existing creator profiles and empty profiles allow-lists on existing API keys, then reconciles strict validators for creator_profiles, api_keys, and audit_logs. It is idempotent and never renames or drops a V1 collection. Existing keys retain their unrestricted behavior because an empty profile list means all profiles.

Focused verification:

.venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/unit/test_creator_service.py \
  tests/unit/test_creator_api.py tests/unit/test_creator_mcp.py \
  tests/unit/test_cli_creator.py tests/integration/test_creator_phase1.py -q
.venv/bin/ruff check .
.venv/bin/ruff format --check .
.venv/bin/mypy app

Public documentation snapshot. Use the generated tool/API reference for contracts in this checkout and live capability discovery for your running deployment.

Creator studio (V6 Phase 13)

The console adds creator preferences and pillars, evidence discovery, idea planning, novelty checks, repurposing plans, content-history search, research briefs, supplied drafts, immutable versions and line comparisons, independent review, manual exports/receipts and manually captured metric observations. Creator profiles are communication/corpus boundaries, separate from human roles and V5 agent permission templates. A person or calling agent supplies prose; there is no autonomous writer or publishing-provider integration.

Session-only adapters live under /api/v6/organizations/{org_id}/creator. They call the existing V2/V3 services and repositories directly, without a privileged machine token. Console activation still requires the earlier verified isolation, identity and policy cutovers. No new dependencies, collections or migration versions are added.

Operation Exact current authority
Creator preferences and pillars creator:read / creator:write on the creator profile; metadata permission does not reveal corpus content
Ideas, briefs, drafts, versions, metrics, discovery, novelty, history and repurposing content:read / content:write for the profile and every transitive linked project/source; unlinked knowledge and skills retain their explicit resource dimensions
Advisory safety scan content:read; it does not change lifecycle or approve
Approval content:write, readable evidence, reviews:decide for the profile, independent verified authorship and exact current revision
Approved manual export content:read and current approved/published revision; there is no invented content:export scope
Manual publication receipt Separate content:publish, current approved revision, explicit confirmation and recent MFA

Every action retains tenant and action/resource coupling through the shared repository envelope. Linked briefs, ideas, skills, research projects and citations are resolved in the same organization, including their linked projects and private-memory boundaries. Lists use bounded tenant/filter/policy cursors (default 20, maximum 50). History search uses the existing lexical/vector candidate prefilters, defensive ownership checks and an explicit token budget. It does not record query terms in workforce monitoring. Search results and advisory comparisons are bounded evidence, not exhaustive history guarantees.

Research brief requests select stored claim IDs and (claim_id, citation_id) keys. The server resolves actual claims, citations, snapshots and locators and revalidates them through the existing research integration service. A caller cannot replace their evidence with invented citation objects. The browser shows retained evidence, source links, factual review state and authored confidence separately. Structured preparation/repurpose results are planning inputs, not newly generated drafts.

Body changes create immutable versions and return content to drafting, clearing its current publication receipt. Authorial metadata changes also invalidate review; editing cannot be combined with approval. Published prose requires a new body version before metadata editing. Record revision and body version are separate labels. Conflicts preserve unsaved prose in component memory and require explicit comparison with the current server revision before retry. Line comparison is bounded to 400 lines per version; full stored text remains available in paged history. Markdown uses the existing allowlisted renderer; HTML/scripts/embeds and unsafe URL schemes are inert.

Managed approval gates remain shared by V2 REST, V6 and capable clients. Normal machines cannot review with content:write. A separately approved service reviewer needs current custody, reviewer grants and independent immutable user/event-time sponsor authorship; using another client of the same sponsor does not create an independent reviewer. The currently shipped MCP publication review tool is advisory and cannot approve; its publication tool still requires separate publish authority. No new MCP administration or approval tool is added.

The shipped manual publisher makes no network request and records no verified external URL/ID. The screen confirms an outside-console action and labels the local receipt-recording time; it does not claim provider confirmation. Export returns formatted text with Cache-Control: no-store, writes no server file, and copies only after an explicit user action. LinkedIn, Medium and GitHub are format choices, never external destinations called by this console.

Metrics are descriptive manual observations with capture time, source and escaped notes. No automatic provider telemetry, productivity/cost inference or causal analytics are promised. Creator audit is content-free and best effort, matching ordinary domain audit. It records the verified human actor; the legacy required key_id field uses unauthenticated to mean no API key, not the human's authentication state. The server-owned audit append checks organization ownership and the current session/policy fence and grants no audit-read/corpus authority. Governance audit retains its separate transactional requirement.

Verification

python -m pytest -q tests/unit/test_v6_creator_adapters.py tests/unit/test_v6_review_authority.py
python -m pytest -q tests/unit/test_content_api.py tests/unit/test_content_discovery.py tests/unit/test_content_novelty.py tests/unit/test_content_retrieval.py tests/unit/test_content_publication.py tests/unit/test_content_publishing.py tests/unit/test_content_metrics.py tests/unit/test_content_research_service.py
V6_CREATOR_ADAPTERS_ONLY=1 bash scripts/test-v6-isolation.sh
npm --prefix dashboard run test:unit -- src/creator/versions.test.tsx src/creator/review.test.tsx src/creator/receipts.test.tsx
npm --prefix dashboard run build
npm --prefix dashboard run test:e2e -- e2e/creator.spec.ts

The integration runner selects test_v6_creator_adapters.py and test_v6_review_authority.py against disposable MongoDB/mongot. Repeated logical IDs have different private tenant sentinels. Approval fixtures create real server-recorded authorship and separately approved service custody, rather than injecting prefiltered provenance. Connected stdio/HTTP MCP clients verify the advisory/approval and publishing boundaries. Browser journeys use the built SPA, real HTTPS API, persisted sessions and synthetic users/factors through the existing private fixture channel. They produce actual revisions, decisions, exports and local receipts without contacting publishing providers. Browser engine/version and measured results belong in each run's evidence; no untested engine coverage is implied. Planning, Graphify output, screenshots and disposable infrastructure artifacts remain ignored and outside public release inventories.

docs/dashboard-deployment.mdPublic documentation

Public documentation snapshot. Use the generated tool/API reference for contracts in this checkout and live capability discovery for your running deployment.

Console deployment and distribution

Release readiness is not approved. See verification and known limits for the outstanding complete acceptance gate. The following describes implemented deployment behavior, not permission to deploy.

The implemented console lives in dashboard/ in this repository. It shares one HTTPS origin with session-only /api/v6, the existing bearer APIs and /mcp. The optional public marketing/documentation site is a separate static host: it has no admin cookie, API upstream, runtime data or secret mounts. Use a different hostname for that site; do not proxy it into this origin.

Build and TLS ingress

Build from a reviewed checkout with Docker Compose 2.24.4 or later (!reset and !override are used). Provision the pinned Python wheels (or preload the reviewed offline cache), then:

./scripts/prepare-docker-wheels.sh
docker compose -f docker-compose.yml -f deploy/console/compose.yml build context-api console

The console target uses digest-pinned Node 24.22.0, npm ci and the committed lockfile, license inventory, TypeScript and build-budget checks. It copies static assets and notices into digest-pinned unprivileged nginx. No Node server, browser bundle secret, CDN, runtime npm install or VITE_* variable is used. The API runtime receives Git/GSSAPI/CA files plus Debian notices from a matching pinned Debian 13 Python image; its build does not resolve mutable apt packages or need Debian mirrors. Python dependencies still use the exact offline wheel lock. When updating either Python base, review them together and rebuild/run the gate.

Set these non-secret deployment values in your private environment:

CONSOLE_SERVER_NAME=console.example.test
CONSOLE_BIND_IP=127.0.0.1
CONSOLE_HTTPS_PORT=8443
V6_BROWSER_ORIGIN=https://console.example.test:8443
CONSOLE_CERT_FILE=./secrets/console-chain.crt
CONSOLE_KEY_FILE=./secrets/console.key
V6_MFA_KEYRING_SECRET=./secrets/v6-mfa-keyring.json
V6_OIDC_REGISTRATIONS_SECRET=./secrets/v6-oidc-registrations.json
V6_PROVIDER_CA_DIRECTORY=./secrets/provider-ca
V6_MAIL_HOST_DIRECTORY=./secrets/mail-handoff

Use lowercase ASCII hostnames and omit :443 for the default HTTPS port. The hostname and external port must match the exact browser origin, certificate SAN and provider callback registration. DNS hostnames and IPv4 SAN certificates are supported; e.g. 127.0.0.1 with a locally trusted development CA. This template does not support IPv6 literal server names. Trust the issuing CA on clients; production browsers must not use an ignored certificate error. For remote use, set an explicit host bind address and DNS/certificate, with the firewall exposing only this TLS port. No public HTTP listener or HTTP password/MCP administration is installed. A remote client uses https://host[:port]/mcp; stdio retains its private API service path and the same current credential/sponsor checks.

The overlay removes all API host ports, enables all prerequisite V6 flags, and trusts only CONSOLE_PROXY_IP (default 172.29.15.2) on a dedicated internal CONSOLE_SUBNET (172.29.15.0/28). If this overlaps another network, change the subnet, proxy and API IPs together. The gateway also joins a separate console_public network for its published TLS port; the API does not join that network. No wildcard proxy trust is accepted. The edge overwrites forwarded scheme/address headers, rejects other Host values, passes API/MCP errors without interception and disables proxy caches/buffering. The app rechecks HTTPS, cookie/bearer separation, CSRF/Origin and current policy. An external load balancer is not implicitly trusted: this template terminates TLS directly; changing that topology needs a new reviewed trust configuration.

The console overlay sets MONGODB_MIN_POOL_SIZE=50 and retains the bounded MONGODB_MAX_POOL_SIZE=50. The driver maintains ready connections for concurrent authenticated directory work; base API/CLI configuration keeps a minimum of zero. Budget these pools per API process and replica-set server, and tune both values together for the installation. A minimum above the maximum refuses startup. This caches connections, never authority or identity records. See the official PyMongo pool configuration.

Only /console/ extensionless navigation uses the SPA fallback. Missing files, /console/assets/*, APIs, MCP and other paths retain their errors. HTML and API responses are no-store; successful hashed assets are immutable, while failed asset requests are no-store.
