Claims are explicit assessments with one of unreviewed, supported, partially_supported, contested, unsupported, or outdated, and optional caller-supplied confidence/rationale. Revision-guarded updates reject stale edits. Neither a note nor a claim automatically creates durable memory.

Citations, packets, and briefs

POST /api/v3/research/citations stores a claim, source, immutable snapshot, optional chunk, locator, evidence excerpt, and relation: supports, contradicts, qualifies, or background. A chunk-backed excerpt must occur in the cited chunk. Locators preserve source-supported page, line, URL/anchor, path, and commit details.

POST /api/v3/research/evidence builds a read-only packet of relevant context, supporting/contradicting/qualifying evidence, locators, dates/classes, and uncertainties. Relations come from persisted citations, not semantic similarity. Conflicting evidence appears together rather than being silently resolved. The claim-evidence route exposes the same authorized evidence for a selected claim.

POST /api/v3/research/briefs stores structured findings, claim/citation references, contradictions, unknowns, and next questions. Missing evidence and bounded-result limits remain visible. The calling agent can write prose from this material; a stored brief is not a guarantee of completeness or correctness.

Candidates, promotion, and skill proposals

POST /api/v3/knowledge-candidates creates a pending_review proposal with explicit target, provenance, confidence, and grants. Approve/reject routes require an expected revision and append immutable decision events. Approval alone makes no change to memory, project context, or canonical skills.

The separate /knowledge-candidates/{candidate_id}/promote route requires an approved revision and supports memory, project_context, and architecture_decision targets. It reuses the ordinary knowledge services, retaining candidate, claim, citation, source, and verification metadata. An explicitly selected old context record may be superseded after the replacement is created; records are not silently deleted. Unsupported target types fail rather than being redirected to another domain.

Skill proposals retain trust_level: generated, an exact current skill version, proposed Markdown patch, rationale, and evidence. They can be inspected/exported, but cannot edit files, commit Git, activate a version, or mutate imported skills. The workflow is proposal -> human review -> canonical Git change -> normal import.

Freshness and content integration

Research-derived knowledge retains verification time, source snapshots, optional review_after, and stable/version-dependent/time-sensitive/volatile freshness metadata. Revalidation identifies due reviews and later changed snapshots, then creates a pending-review update candidate. A changed hash or source version is a review signal; it does not automatically invalidate, overwrite, or promote knowledge.

Creator briefs can retain research claims and citations. Content fact review maps a saved draft to explicitly stored claims and evidence, reporting supported, unsupported, contested, outdated, and unmapped material. It does not rewrite the draft, guarantee truth, or publish it. See content-schema.md.

MCP, CLI, and operations

MCP exposes constrained research capabilities such as project/source registration, manual text or registered repository ingestion, research search, notes/claims, evidence packets, briefs, candidates, and skill proposals. It has no arbitrary URL-fetch, filesystem-read, shell, Git-command, or database-query tool. Web acquisition and uploaded file bytes use the REST/operator CLI boundary.

CLI groups include research, source, note, claim, candidate, and skill proposal; use contextctl <group> --help and cli.md for current arguments. The runnable research example and usage guide walk through the full sequence.

Source-count, shared ingestion-concurrency, and per-ingestion chunk limits bound expensive work. Failed capacity checks return safe errors without queuing work. Full-database backups include research snapshots, evidence, review history, and promotion metadata. Respect the source's license and disclosure rights when storing excerpts or exporting research-derived content.

docs/retrieval.mdPublic documentation

Public documentation snapshot. Use the generated tool/API reference for contracts in this checkout and live capability discovery for your running deployment.

Retrieval

Retrieval has three modes: vector search for conceptual similarity, lexical search for exact technical vocabulary, and hybrid retrieval, which runs both, combines their scores, and returns a token-budgeted context. Vector and lexical search are served by self-managed mongot; all three resolve the same metadata filters.

Unified knowledge search is the interface built on top of them: POST /api/v1/search runs this pipeline across eligible core knowledge sources and is documented in search.md. This page documents the machinery it is made of.

This core pipeline retrieves three collections. Skill chunks are global knowledge available to permitted readers. Project context belongs to one authorized project; projects.md describes its isolation rules. Memory supports shared global/project records and authenticated agent or project-agent records; memory.md explains ownership and supersession. Creator-content and research retrieval use separate domain workflows.

Topology

Context API ──► mongod ──► mongot ──► vector index + search index

The application issues createSearchIndexes, $listSearchIndexes, $vectorSearch, and $search to mongod, which coordinates with mongot. No application code opens a connection to mongot, and no mongot endpoint is configured anywhere in the application settings. No other search engine is involved.

Indexes

Six core-knowledge search indexes exist — one Vector Search and one Search index over each core collection — reconciled by the same primitives in app/db/search_indexes.py.

Vector index

Property Value
Name skill_chunk_vector_index
Type vectorSearch
Path embedding
numDimensions The dimensions of the loaded embedding model
similarity cosine
Filter fields skill_id, skill_version

Dimensions have exactly one source: the model the embedding provider actually loaded. Startup loads the model, reads EmbeddingModelInfo.dimensions from it, and passes that to ensure_vector_indexes(). Because the embedding provider refuses to load a model whose real dimensions differ from EMBEDDING_DIMENSIONS, the configured value, the stored vectors, and the index can never disagree. There is no separate vector-dimension setting to drift.

Cosine matches the normalized unit vectors the provider produces. Changing it requires evidence from retrieval evaluation, not preference.

Search index

Property Value
Name skill_chunk_text_index
Type search
Mapped fields content, section, skill_id, skill_version
Analyzers lucene.standard on content and section; identifier_exact on content.exact
Filter fields skill_id, skill_version (indexed as token)

content is indexed twice. The standard analyzer handles ordinary prose and punctuation, so Keycloak. at the end of a sentence still matches Keycloak. The identifier_exact multi-field uses a whitespace tokenizer with a lowercase filter, so wallet:read, /api/v1/payments, payment-service, and INSUFFICIENT_SCOPE survive tokenization as single terms rather than being split at every symbol. Matching is case-insensitive; structure is not.

dynamic: false keeps vectors and internal fields out of the text index.

Project context indexes

Property Value
Names project_context_vector_index, project_context_text_index
Vector path embedding, cosine, dimensions from the loaded model
Mapped text content (with the same exact multi-field), title
Filter fields project_id, type, status, tags, importance

A context document carries its own metadata, so every filter — project isolation included — is a pre-filter on the same document rather than a scope resolved from another collection. The title is indexed at a 1.5 boost: it states what the entry is about, which is a stronger signal than a section heading inside a longer document.

The analyzer, the exact multi-field, and the query shape are shared with skill chunks, so one lexical vocabulary governs both collections.

Memory indexes

Property Value
Names memory_vector_index, memory_text_index
Vector path embedding, cosine, dimensions from the loaded model
Mapped text content (with the same exact multi-field), summary
Filter fields scope, project_id, client_id, type, status, tags, importance

Memory search unions the eligible scopes in its pre-filter: shared global records, the explicitly named project's records, and the authenticated client's own agent/project-agent records where applicable. Each branch retains its project and client ownership conditions. The summary is boosted at 1.5: it states the memory in one line, which matches a question more directly than the body it condenses.

Managed search intersects the search action with each source's read action. Impossible NONE branches are removed without widening their AND/OR predicate. ALL resource identifiers use a nonempty string range inside mongot, equivalent to their strict identifier schema; they do not enumerate every corpus ObjectId. Both vector prefilters and lexical string ranges retain the explicit organization condition. More complex provenance predicates still use bounded ID preselection and refuse work beyond that bound. Retrieved ownership and action/resource access are checked independently afterward.

Index reconciliation

ensure_vector_indexes() and ensure_text_indexes() are safe to run on every startup and every import:

  1. Absent index: created.
  2. Identical definition: left untouched.
  3. Different path, dimensions, similarity, analyzer, or mapped fields: updated in place, which makes an embedding-model migration a configuration change rather than a manual operation.

Only the parts of a definition this application controls are compared, so defaults MongoDB adds to a stored definition never cause a pointless rebuild on the next startup.

A concurrent creation race resolves to "unchanged". Every failure to reach the search coordinator raises SearchUnavailableError, which startup logs as vector_index_unavailable without stopping the process; /health/ready then reports the platform as not ready.

Search indexes are not part of the migration history and are not backed up: they are derived state that can always be rebuilt from the stored vectors.

Filters

$vectorSearch can only pre-filter on fields indexed on the same collection, and chunks carry no skill metadata. The retrieval service therefore resolves metadata filters against the skills collection first and passes the resulting (skill_id, skill_version) keys into the query:

category / tags / trust_level / active  ──► skills ──► version keys ──► $vectorSearch filter

Vector search pre-filters inside the approximate search, which keeps limit results reachable; filtering after a k-nearest-neighbour query would silently return fewer results than requested. Lexical search applies the same keys as compound.filter clauses, which restrict what is eligible without contributing to relevance. Supported filters:

Filter Behaviour
skill_id One skill
skill_version One exact version; requires skill_id
category Exact match
tags Skill must carry every requested tag
trust_level trusted, user, external, or generated
active_only Default true; ignored when skill_version is given

Requesting an explicit version targets that version even when it is superseded, which is the same rule the skill detail endpoint follows. Beyond 200 matching versions the pre-filter stops being selective, so the query runs unfiltered and over-fetches instead; every result is verified against the resolved set either way, so a result outside the filter can never be returned.

Lexical relevance

A lexical query becomes one compound operator whose clauses each contribute score:

Clause Path Boost Purpose
text content.exact 3.0 The identifier matched exactly as written
phrase content 2.0 The words appeared together, in order
text content 1.0 Ordinary prose matching
text section 0.5 The heading mentioned the term

An exact identifier match is the strongest signal lexical search has, so it carries the largest boost. These are deliberate starting weights for retrieval evaluation, not optimal values; hybrid ranking weights are configurable.

Setting phrase: true promotes the phrase clause from optional to required, so only chunks containing the words together, in order, match at all. Without it a phrase still boosts the chunks that contain it, while chunks containing only the individual words remain eligible.

The query text reaches the analyzers exactly as written apart from whitespace normalization: casing, colons, slashes, dots, and underscores are preserved, because destroying them is what makes wallet:read unfindable.

Results

Both modes return the same model, so a caller handles one shape regardless of how a result was found:

{
  "source": "skill_chunk",
  "method": "lexical",
  "score": 2.848,
  "skill": {"skill_id": "fastapi-production", "version": "1.0.0", "category": "backend", "..." : "..."},
  "chunk": {"chunk_id": "chunk-0000", "section": "Rules", "content": "..."}
}

method distinguishes a cosine similarity (roughly 0..1) from a lexical relevance score (unbounded, comparable only within one query). The two are never mixed in this shape; combining them is what hybrid retrieval does, after normalizing both.

Vectors are never returned to clients. Internal BSON identifiers and revisions are not exposed.

numCandidates for vector search is derived from the requested limit: limit × VECTOR_SEARCH_CANDIDATE_MULTIPLIER, clamped by VECTOR_SEARCH_MAX_CANDIDATES and by MongoDB's own ceiling, and never below limit.

Hybrid retrieval

Vector search finds what a question means; lexical search finds what it literally says. Neither is sufficient alone: a vector query for wallet:read drifts to whatever is conceptually nearby, and a lexical query for "how do we avoid charging twice" matches nothing. Hybrid retrieval runs both and combines them.

query ──┬─► vector search ──┐
        └─► lexical search ─┴─► merge ─► filter ─► rank ─► deduplicate ─► token budget ─► context

Both searches run concurrently over the same resolved metadata scope, so hybrid retrieval costs roughly one round trip rather than two.

Module boundaries

app/retrieval/ holds the algorithm and imports nothing from app/db/ or app/repositories/:

Module Responsibility
query.py Query normalization, the first stage of every pipeline
types.py The candidate, score, and diagnostics value objects
filters.py What a request may see, including project isolation
ranking.py Normalization, the weighted score, deterministic ordering
hybrid.py Merging the two result sets and removing duplicates
context_builder.py Filling the token budget and shaping the result

RetrievalService is the only piece that knows about both. It splits into two halves that compose: gather_sources() resolves each source's scope and runs both searches against each one concurrently, returning source-agnostic candidates; rank_context() performs no I/O at all and turns candidates into budgeted context. hybrid_search() and unified knowledge search are both those two calls in sequence, which is why one ranking implementation serves both. Ranking can therefore be exercised, and retrieval quality evaluated, without MongoDB running.

Score normalization

The two scores are not comparable as they stand, so each is normalized against what it means:

Score Range Normalization
Vector 0..1 (cosine, reported by MongoDB) Clamped; it already carries an absolute meaning
Lexical Unbounded, query-specific Divided by the best score of its own source's search

Relative scaling is used for lexical scores rather than min-max, because min-max always reports the weakest result as a total mismatch and inflates differences that carry no meaning. Dividing by the best score preserves the ratios between results.

Lexical scores are scaled within each source. A score reflects the statistics of the index it came from, so a skill chunk's relevance and a context entry's relevance only become comparable after each is scaled against the best result of its own search; scaling them together would rank one collection's index statistics against another's. Cosine similarity needs no such treatment: the same model and metric produce it in both collections, so it is comparable as it stands.

A result only one search found contributes nothing from the other, so agreement between the two searches ranks above a single strong hit. When a search did not run at all — no embedding model is loaded — its weight is redistributed over the remaining signals instead, because scoring every result against a signal that cannot exist would only compress the scores.

Ranking

final_score = 0.45 * vector_score
            + 0.25 * lexical_score
            + 0.15 * importance_score
            + 0.10 * recency_score
            + 0.05 * source_priority
Weight Setting Default
Vector similarity RETRIEVAL_WEIGHT_VECTOR 0.45
Lexical relevance RETRIEVAL_WEIGHT_LEXICAL 0.25
Importance RETRIEVAL_WEIGHT_IMPORTANCE 0.15
Recency RETRIEVAL_WEIGHT_RECENCY 0.10
Source priority RETRIEVAL_WEIGHT_SOURCE_PRIORITY 0.05

Weights express relative influence and are normalized before use, so any configuration keeps the final score inside 0..1 and comparable between queries. These are starting values for retrieval evaluation, not measured optima.

Source priority encodes that project-specific knowledge should normally beat generic knowledge:

Source Priority
project_context 1.00
active_skill 0.95
memory 0.80
conversation 0.50

Skills, project context, and memory are wired up; a conversation is stored but carries no index, so nothing retrieves one yet. Asking for it is answered rather than rejected: unified search reports it under skipped_sources. Project context is the reason the source term exists: at equal relevance it beats an active skill, which is what "project-specific information should normally beat generic knowledge" means in practice. Memory sits below both — useful across sessions, but less authoritative than what a project recorded about itself.

Importance is a curator-assigned value. Project context and memory carry a real one, chosen by whoever stored the entry; skills carry none, so every skill chunk scores neutrally and the term separates one entry from another within those sources. Recency halves every RETRIEVAL_RECENCY_HALF_LIFE_DAYS (default 90) from the document's updated_at — for a skill, when that version was imported; for context or memory, when it was last edited.

A memory's confidence is stored and returned but is not a ranking term: adding a sixth signal to the documented formula is a change that should follow retrieval evaluation, not precede it.

Ranking is deterministic. The reference time is passed in rather than read from a clock, scores are summed in a fixed order and rounded before they are compared, and ties are broken by source priority, then an active version over a superseded one, then newer content, then the stable candidate key. The same inputs in any order produce the same output.

Deduplication

After ranking, a result is dropped when a better-ranked result already covers its content: the share of the shorter result's words that also appear in the longer one reaches RETRIEVAL_DUPLICATE_OVERLAP (default 0.85). Because the better-ranked copy is the one kept, and ranking already prefers active and newer versions, the surviving copy is the one worth keeping.

The chunker deliberately repeats 50-100 tokens between adjacent chunks. That overlap is roughly a tenth of a chunk, far below the threshold, so genuinely different neighbours both survive while a chunk contained in another — or the same section reachable through two skill versions — is returned once. Results shorter than a dozen distinct words are only removed when they repeat exactly, since short fragments share common words by chance.

Token budget

The platform stores a lot and retrieves little. RETRIEVAL_TOKEN_BUDGET (default 4000) is filled in rank order and RETRIEVAL_MAX_TOKEN_BUDGET (default 16000) is the ceiling a request may ask for: a caller can request less context, never more than the deployment allows.

A result that does not fit is skipped and a smaller later one may still be included, so one oversized result cannot waste the budget. Content is never truncated: half a technical rule reads like a whole one, which is worse than omitting it. A budget smaller than the largest matching chunk therefore returns fewer results, or none, by design.

Explainable metadata

Every result carries its score breakdown — each normalized signal, the raw scores, and which searches found it — and every response carries pipeline counters: how many matches each search returned, how many merged, how many the filters removed, how many were duplicates, and how many were dropped for budget. This stays internal by default and is returned only when a request asks for it, so a surprising ranking is reproducible instead of a guess without making every response larger.

API

POST /api/v1/skills/search/vector
{
  "query": "How do we prevent duplicate payment requests?",
  "category": "backend",
  "tags": ["payments"],
  "trust_level": "trusted",
  "active_only": true,
  "limit": 5
}

The response reports the active embedding model and dimensions alongside the ranked results.

POST /api/v1/skills/search/lexical
{
  "query": "wallet:read",
  "phrase": false,
  "category": "security",
  "limit": 5
}

Lexical search needs no embedding model, so it keeps working with EMBEDDING_ENABLED=false and while the model is still loading. Both endpoints return 503 when their infrastructure cannot serve the query, with a message that exposes no internals, and 422 for a malformed request. POST /api/v1/search combines eligible core knowledge sources; these three remain for callers that want exactly one kind of knowledge or one retrieval method.

POST /api/v1/skills/search/hybrid
{
  "query": "How do we prevent duplicate payment requests?",
  "project_id": "payment-service",
  "category": "backend",
  "minimum_importance": 0.0,
  "token_budget": 4000,
  "limit": 10,
  "explain": false
}

The response is the budgeted context rather than raw search results:

{
  "query": "How do we prevent duplicate payment requests?",
  "project_id": "payment-service",
  "token_count": 900,
  "token_budget": 4000,
  "results": [
    {
      "source": "active_skill",
      "title": "Payment Service: Idempotency",
      "content": "...",
      "score": 0.9225,
      "tokens": 300,
      "metadata": {"skill_id": "payment-service", "skill_version": "1.0.0", "...": "..."}
    }
  ]
}

explain: true fills in the explanation on each result and the diagnostics on the response; both keys are always present and null otherwise, so the response shape never varies. Hybrid retrieval degrades to its lexical half with EMBEDDING_ENABLED=false, reporting the weighting it actually applied.

POST /api/v1/skills/search remains a literal metadata/content search: it matches escaped literal terms with regular expressions over skill metadata and chunk content, needs no search index, and returns no scores. It remains useful when mongot is unavailable.

Project isolation

Runtime skills and chunks are tenant-owned imports without a project_id; their organization-global policy is explicit, not an installation-shared fallback. Memory can also belong to an authenticated client. The filters preserve these ownership boundaries on every candidate:

  • Organization-imported skills and organization-global memory require their explicit permitted resources.
  • Content owned by a project is visible only to that project.
  • A request naming no project cannot retrieve project context or project memory.
  • An authenticated client can retrieve only its own agent-scoped memory. Project-agent memory also requires its explicit authorized project.

The rule is applied three times over, because one layer failing must not become a leak: the repository is bound to trusted organization/project, the search pre-filters on org_id and action-specific resources inside the query, and the service checks every candidate again before ranking. None of the three trusts the caller to have scoped the query correctly. projects.md and memory.md document the rest of the isolation contract.

Readiness

/health/ready reports both indexes:

{
  "vector_search": {
    "enabled": true,
    "available": true,
    "index": "skill_chunk_vector_index",
    "queryable": true,
    "index_status": "READY",
    "dimensions": 384,
    "dimensions_match": true
  },
  "lexical_search": {
    "available": true,
    "index": "skill_chunk_text_index",
    "queryable": true,
    "index_status": "READY",
    "analyzer": "lucene.standard"
  }
}

Two more blocks, context_search and memory_search, report the project-context and memory index pairs the same way; see projects.md and memory.md.

Retrieval logging

Every unified search reports what it did to a hook when it finishes: always to the structured log, and — with RETRIEVAL_LOG_ENABLED=true — to the retrieval_logs collection as well. The query text never reaches the application log. search.md documents both hooks and why storing a query is opt-in.

Readiness fails while any index is missing, still building, or unreachable, and while a vector index was built for a different number of dimensions than the loaded model. With EMBEDDING_ENABLED=false no provider is built and vector search stops being a required dependency; the Search indexes are still required, because lexical retrieval does not depend on the model.

Verification

python -m pytest                                   # unit coverage, no MongoDB required
docker compose --profile test run --rm --build test  # live mongod + mongot checks

The live checks build both indexes, wait for mongot to report them queryable, and then assert ranking, every supported filter, top-K bounds, score ordering, and idempotent reconciliation. Vector coverage inserts chunks whose vectors point along known axes. Lexical coverage inserts chunks containing Keycloak, OAuth2, wallet:read, INSUFFICIENT_SCOPE, /api/v1/payments, payment-service, PostgreSQL, Redis, Saga, outbox, PaymentIdempotencyService, FastAPI, and MONGODB_REPLICA_SET, then asserts that each one retrieves the chunk that contains it.

Hybrid coverage points the query vector at one chunk's axis and puts the technical identifiers in another, so a result can only reach the top on evidence the ranking actually combined: it asserts that agreement wins, that an exact identifier lifts a chunk above a closer vector match, that the token budget bounds what comes back, and that repeating a query against live indexes returns identical scores. Project-context coverage asserts that neither a context search nor hybrid retrieval reaches another project's entries, and that a request naming no project reaches none of them at all. Memory coverage asserts the same for project memory, and that global memory reaches every request.

docs/search.mdPublic documentation

Public documentation snapshot. Use the generated tool/API reference for contracts in this checkout and live capability discovery for your running deployment.

Unified knowledge search

All runtime records and search candidates described here belong to one trusted organization. global means organization-global, with explicit action/resource policy; it never means a null-org or cross-installation corpus. Imported skills are tenant-owned copies of canonical Git. Private agent memory also retains verified client ownership and is not revealed by human management visibility.

POST /api/v1/search

One question, every source that can answer it. Skills, a project's own recorded context, and memory are searched together, ranked against each other, and cut to a token budget — rather than asked three times and concatenated by the caller.

The individual skill, context, and memory search endpoints remain available. They remain the right tool when a caller wants exactly one kind of knowledge, or when it needs the stored record rather than retrieved context. This is the interface for the case that matters most: a question, and the context that answers it.

The pipeline

query
  │
  ▼  normalize          whitespace collapsed; identifiers, casing and symbols untouched
  ▼  select sources     a source not asked for is never searched
  ▼  embed              one query vector, reused by every vector search
  ├──────────────┬──────────────┐
  ▼ skills       ▼ context      ▼ memory        each searched lexically and by vector,
  └──────────────┴──────────────┘                all concurrently
  ▼  filter             project isolation, sources, tags, importance, lifecycle
  ▼  rank               the shared ranking formula, across requested sources
  ▼  deduplicate        a result a better-ranked one already covers is dropped
  ▼  token budget       filled in rank order, nothing truncated
  ▼  context builder
  ▼  compact response   content, source metadata, score, and retrieval metadata

Every stage is the one the individual searches already use: RetrievalService runs the searches, app/retrieval/ ranks and budgets what they return. A unified answer therefore cannot rank differently from the endpoint it replaces — there is one ranking implementation, not two.

Sources

Source What it is Priority Reachable
project_context What a project recorded about itself 1.00 Inside its own project
active_skill Curated skill chunks, carrying their skill's metadata 0.95 Everywhere
memory Eligible shared and authenticated client-operational memory 0.80 Per memory.md
conversation Stored, but carries no index yet 0.50 Not retrievable

Naming no source searches everything retrievable. sources narrows that, and does so twice: a source that was not asked for is never searched, and is refused again at the filter, so one of the two failing cannot put it in an answer.

A conversation can be asked for and is answered honestly rather than rejected: conversations are stored separately but carry no vector and no search index, so conversation always appears under skipped_sources. Conversation records are not automatically embedded or extracted into memory.

active_skill covers both "skills" and "skill chunks": a skill is retrieved as the chunk that answers the question, carrying the metadata of the skill version it came from.

Filters

Filter Applies to Behaviour
project_id Everything The isolation boundary; see below
sources Everything Which kinds of knowledge may answer
tags Everything The result must carry every requested tag
minimum_importance Everything Skills score neutrally at 0.5
active_only Everything Default true; excludes archived and superseded
phrase Everything The query words must appear together, in order
context_types Project context One or more of the fourteen types
memory_types Memory preference, convention, …
memory_scopes Memory Eligible subset of global, project, agent, project_agent
skill_id / skill_version Skills One skill, or one exact version
category / trust_level Skills Skill metadata

skill_id, skill_version, category, and trust_level describe a skill. No context entry and no memory carries one, so naming any of them makes the request a request about skills: the other sources are reported as skipped rather than searched, returning candidates that the same filter would then discard. Skipping them says what happened; searching them would read exactly like both sources being empty.

memory_scopes narrows the eligible scopes and cannot widen ownership. Project scopes require an explicit authorized project; agent scopes require a linked authenticated client. Defaults include global memory, the named project's memory when present, and that client's own operational scopes when authenticated. See memory.md.

Project isolation

Unified search preserves both project and client ownership:

  • Global knowledge is shared with callers holding the required grants.
  • Knowledge owned by a project is visible only to that project.
  • A request naming no project cannot retrieve project context or project memory.
  • Agent memory is visible only to its authenticated client; naming a project also makes that client's own project-agent memory eligible.
  • Research and creator-content collections use their dedicated search workflows; this endpoint searches core skills, context, and memory.

It is enforced three times over, and unified search deliberately re-states it rather than assuming the sources enforced it: each repository is bound to its scope when it is built, each search pre-filters on project_id inside the query, and the service checks every candidate again before ranking. A result belonging to another project is dropped even if a search returns it.

Retrieval metadata

Every response carries a retrieval block. It is not behind explain, because an answer drawn from several sources is only debuggable if the caller can see which ones contributed:

{
  "query_id": "0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef",
  "retrieval_method": "hybrid",
  "requested_sources": ["project_context", "active_skill", "memory"],
  "searched_sources": ["active_skill", "memory"],
  "skipped_sources": ["project_context"],
  "latency_ms": 18.41,
  "diagnostics": {
    "methods": ["vector", "lexical"],
    "weights": {"vector": 0.45, "lexical": 0.25, "...": 0.0},
    "vector_matches": 6, "lexical_matches": 3, "merged": 7,
    "filtered_out": 1, "duplicates_removed": 1, "ranked": 5,
    "dropped_for_budget": 2
  }
}

skipped_sources is what turns an empty answer into an explanation: a source contributes nothing either because it found nothing, or because no query ran against it at all. retrieval_method is hybrid when both searches ran and names the survivor when only one did, so a deployment running without an embedding model is visible in its own output rather than indistinguishable from a healthy one.

Per-result score breakdowns stay behind explain: true. They are the part that grows with the answer; the block above is a fixed size.

Results

{
  "key": "project_context:payment-service:6720a1b2c3d4e5f60718293a",
  "source": "project_context",
  "title": "Payment idempotency strategy",
  "content": "Every charge request carries a UUID4 idempotency key. …",
  "score": 0.8343,
  "tokens": 28,
  "metadata": {"context_id": "…", "project_id": "payment-service", "type": "architecture_decision"}
}

key identifies a result stably across queries, so a caller can say which result it used and a retrieval log can record the same thing. metadata carries the source's own fields — a skill's id, version, section and trust level; a context entry's type and importance; a memory's scope, confidence, and both ends of any supersession.

Nothing is unbounded: limit is at most 50, the token budget is clamped to the deployment's maximum, and content is never truncated to fit — a result that does not fit is left out whole.

Retrieval logging

Every search is reported to a hook when it finishes. app/search/logging.py defines the entry and the protocol; a hook that fails is logged and skipped, because retrieval logging exists to explain searches and must never be the reason one fails.

Two hooks exist:

Hook Records Default
StructuredRetrievalLogger One retrieval_completed log line Always on
PersistentRetrievalLogger One retrieval_logs document RETRIEVAL_LOG_ENABLED

The structured line carries query_id, project_id, retrieval_method, requested_sources, result_count, and latency_ms — and deliberately not the query text. That is the one field in a search that can describe the person who ran it, and application logs are shipped, indexed, and retained by whatever collects stdout.

Storing it is therefore opt-in. With RETRIEVAL_LOG_ENABLED=true each search also writes one retrieval_logs document holding query, project, requested sources, result count, selected result keys, latency, and method. Results are referenced by key rather than copied, so the record stays small and reading it back cannot become a second way to read the knowledge base. The document is written inside the project scope the search ran in.

A finished search also tells the call it is part of what it did — the query identifier, the project, and the result count — so the one HTTP access line for that request carries them too, and records acp_retrieval_duration_seconds and acp_retrieval_results. Each index query underneath is timed separately as acp_search_duration_seconds{method,collection}, and a query that could not be served is counted as acp_search_failures_total{method,collection}: vector and lexical apart, because a rebuilding vector index takes semantic search down while lexical search keeps answering. See observability.md.

API

POST /api/v1/search
{
  "query": "How do we prevent duplicate payment requests?",
  "project_id": "payment-service",
  "sources": ["project_context", "active_skill", "memory"],
  "memory_scopes": ["global", "project"],
  "context_types": ["architecture_decision"],
  "tags": ["payments"],
  "minimum_importance": 0.5,
  "token_budget": 4000,
  "limit": 10,
  "explain": false
}

200 returns the budgeted context. 503 means the search infrastructure or the embedding model could not serve the query, with a message that exposes no internals. 422 rejects a malformed request — an empty query, a limit or budget outside its range, a repeated filter value, a version without its skill, or project memory without a project.

Reaching it from an agent

search_knowledge is the MCP tool over this endpoint, and the one an agent should reach for first. See mcp.md.

Verification

python -m pytest                                     # unit coverage, no MongoDB required
docker compose --profile test run --rm --build test  # live mongod + mongot checks

The live checks seed one skill, two projects' context, and both scopes of memory on known vector axes and with deliberately disjoint vocabulary, then assert that one query reaches all three sources ranked together; that a semantic query with no word in common still retrieves the right context on vector evidence alone; that INSUFFICIENT_SCOPE, wallet:read, /api/v1/payments and OAuth2 each retrieve the chunk containing them despite the query vector pointing elsewhere; that no query reaches another project while each project reaches its own; that a smaller budget removes whole results and alters none of the ones it keeps; that restricting sources restricts what is searched; that repeating a query returns identical scores; and that an opted-in deployment stores exactly one record per search.

docs/security.mdPublic documentation

Public documentation snapshot. Use the generated tool/API reference for contracts in this checkout and live capability discovery for your running deployment.

Security

The platform authorizes sensitive knowledge and authority at the server. Retrieved content is labelled data, not instructions. Verification and known limits records unresolved release blockers; documented controls are not a conformance or capacity certification.

Organization and operator boundaries

All served domain records, imported skills, memory scopes, jobs, counts, joins, search candidates and exports belong to one organization. Missing trusted context fails closed; an org header/path/body selector is never authority. References, provenance and supersession must stay in the same org. Tenant/resource filters apply before lexical/vector selection, with defensive result checks. Cursors bind org, subject, action and filters. Extra organizations remain sealed until explicit activation. See database contracts and isolation.

Logical isolation does not protect stored data from trusted installation database, secret-mount and backup operators. Private global human identities are not tenant directory data. Raw whole-database archives, restore, provider configuration and shared process metrics are installation operations; an org owner is not an installation operator. Authentication-disabled multitenant startup is refused. Public health/readiness does not supply domain authority. No public owner claim, public enrollment, tenant restore or unscoped worker compatibility mode exists.

Browser identity and SSO

Human sessions authenticate only /api/v6. Bearer V1–V5/MCP refuse browser cookies; V6 rejects bearer authentication. Opaque random sessions/challenges are hashed in MongoDB. Cookies are Secure, HttpOnly, host-only, SameSite=Lax; idle and absolute expiry are checked per request. Mutations require exact HTTPS Origin and CSRF, current session/org/policy context and recent MFA for privileged work. Rotation, logout, revoke, org switching and sensitive identity changes invalidate old contexts. No persistent browser token or VITE_* secret is used.

Each authenticated request reads current user, membership and organization authority from the exact stored session bindings, including their epochs and revisions. The internal read join follows the exact hashed session to its verified same-org membership before reading global user and login-identity records. It is not a directory source and never matches email/name. Joined identity rows stay private. Expiry is checked again after authority reads and in the final atomic session update. No authority rows are cached across requests. Session mutations join the exact original context bindings on their existing transaction session; the anchor, user, membership and browser-session write fences remain required. Policy reads use one bounded org-filtered aggregation for the current ancestry inputs, including reads on an existing transaction session. Global users join through same-org membership IDs; row-count, execution-time and MongoDB document-size limits refuse excess work instead of returning partial authority. Installation controls are checked before private joins on ordinary reads and outside an older transaction snapshot on transactional reads. The shared policy anchor still fences revocation against issuance and delivery. This is not a persistent policy cache.

Invitation-only local enrollment uses Argon2id through the maintained password library, with pinned work parameters and bounded concurrency. It does not use the machine-token hash or reversible password encryption. MFA seeds use versioned installation-mounted AES-GCM keys; recovery codes are random hashed, single-use values. Reset leaves MFA and suspended memberships intact. Purpose-bound, expiring challenges consume atomically with identity audit. Delivery is a private local test/operator sink; no production SMTP or real invitation sending is claimed. See local identity.

OIDC uses Authorization Code + S256 PKCE, state/nonce and exact issuer, subject, audience, signature, expiry and redirect checks. Discovery/endpoints are bounded and allowlisted HTTPS, not an arbitrary URL proxy. Equal email never links identities; linking authenticates both with step-up and session invalidation. Provider roles/groups are not platform grants. Required SSO checks the target org's approved registration and trusted assurance; org A login cannot satisfy org B's different provider. Downtime supplies no automatic local fallback. Explicit operator-approved break-glass is bounded and requires local MFA. Provider/account revocation follows documented session/revalidation bounds, not unsupported instant revocation. See SSO contracts.

Roles, grants and review

Every managed permission couples an action to a resource selector: NONE, selected IDs or explicit all_in_org. Empty managed policy grants nothing. Read-A/write-B cannot authorize write-A. Organization-global knowledge/skills need explicit rights; management visibility never implies private agent memory. Role templates only define eligible capabilities. There is no owner corpus bypass.

Children remain within current parent generation, resource/action envelope, allowed targets/roles, depth and expiry. Self-grants, self-ceiling changes, foreign references and last-owner removal fail. Governance mutation and immutable audit/outbox share a replica-set transaction and conditional policy-anchor fence; parent revoke/narrow races child issuance on that same anchor. Reinstatement or widening never resurrects revoked descendants. Ordinary domain audit remains best-effort and is not the governance durability contract.

Content/research review needs operation-specific authority, source readability, exact current revision and verified independent authorship. content:write alone never authorizes managed approval. Normal machines cannot review; a separately approved service-account exception is bounded by custody, review operations/resources, expiry and sponsor-based self-review checks. A second client with the same sponsor is not independent. Promotion and publication have separate permissions; publication records a manual receipt without outbound publishing. See organization management.

Machine credentials and offboarding

A credential has public key ID and 32 random secret bytes; only its SHA-256 hash is stored, compared in constant time. High-entropy machine tokens use a different contract from human passwords. Verified sponsorship/custody is required; old owner_id text is not proof. Legacy keys must be claimed explicitly or revoked before managed activation. A reviewed legacy adapter means all_in_org only in its adoption org, never a cross-org/global admin key.

Approval and issuance are separate. Only the authenticated authorized recipient receives plaintext once. Leads inspect/revoke allowed metadata, never another worker's token. Retries/outbox/idempotency do not replay plaintext. Lost delivery requires revoke/replacement. Template edits/disable do not change assigned clients or keys. Current key/client/sponsor/team/delegation rights intersect per action and resource on REST, stdio and HTTP MCP preflight, including active sessions. Jobs/results recheck current authority; already committed work is not undone. See managed agents and client setup.

Secrets, monitoring and audit

Keep secrets in private mounted files/approved secret storage, never source, images, argv, URLs or browser storage. Back up all retained MFA key versions separately from raw database archives. MongoDB tooling receives passwords via private temporary files. Structured logs have a field allowlist and bounded failure classifications; do not assume every historical log or arbitrary driver trace is safe to publish. Review artifacts before sharing them.

Governance and activity records are content-free. Private retrieval diagnostics may contain search queries and are excluded from workforce monitoring, as are identity audit, prompts, transcripts and response bodies. Event-time sponsor/team labels do not rewrite verified actor identity. Team moves cannot reveal previous team events. Metadata rights do not reveal corpus. Charts declare source, population, timezone, watermark/coverage and unavailable/partial states; process last observations are not historical series or productivity measures.

/metrics requires the separate mounted OPERATOR_METRICS_TOKEN_FILE; a tenant system:read grant is insufficient. Tenant reports have current policy checks, 5-minute expiry, 5,000-row/2 MiB bounds and CSV formula neutralization. Reports are not raw backups. See monitoring, observability and backup.

Report delivery reevaluates natural grant expiry synchronously after its final policy-anchor check, with no subsequent database await. Four real MongoDB cases pass for export/activity expiry during rendering and the final fence. Complete final-source expiry/revocation reconciliation remains required; see verification and known limits before deployment.

Deployment, queries and untrusted rendering

The HTTPS console overlay removes API host ports and trusts only its configured ingress proxy. SPA fallback is restricted to console navigation; API/MCP/missing assets retain errors. API and HTML are no-store; successful hashed assets are immutable. API CSP denies execution/framing; the separate static console permits local scripts/fonts/connect and the styles needed by its primitives, with frame protections and no CDN dependency. The public marketing site is separately hostable with no session/API upstream.

Queries use typed value fields, bounded predicates and escaped search terms; callers cannot supply Mongo operators, shell commands or arbitrary filesystem paths. Strict validators and tenant-first natural-key indexes supplement repository guards. Managed mutations use expected revisions and current policy. Request body, concurrency, auth-work, candidate and pagination limits bound work. Limits are safeguards, not demonstrated throughput promises.

Evidence ingestion retries at most five confirmed-aborted internal storage transactions, with bounded backoff and a fresh session/policy fence each time. Unknown commit outcomes, caller-owned transactions, human review decisions and credential issuance are not automatically replayed by this storage hook. A policy revision change still refuses the operation. This distinguishes MongoDB's transient transaction and unknown commit labels.

Markdown rendering disables raw HTML, scripts and unsafe URL schemes. Research documents remain untrusted evidence. Skills are canonical reviewed Git imports; the console cannot write arbitrary server files or auto-apply proposed patches. The platform cannot make retrieved text safe to follow as privileged instructions.

Research ingestion boundaries

The configured providers constrain acquisition and retained material. These controls require an appropriate deployment network policy when accepting untrusted source submissions.

Boundary Review outcome
URL ingestion Registered HTTP(S) sources only; public-address preflight checks, bounded redirects/time/size, approved content types, and no ambient proxies. A connected peer is checked after response headers where available. DNS results are not pinned to the connection; use outbound restrictions for private and metadata networks.
File/PDF ingestion Bytes only, no paths or execution; MIME/signature checks, parser/page/stream/extracted-text ceilings, unsafe filename, archive, and executable rejection.
Git/GitHub ingestion Fixed argument invocation with a sterile environment; no shell, hooks, checkout, submodules, scripts, code execution, or credentials. File/repository ceilings and binary, symlink, unsafe-path, and likely-secret exclusions apply.
Authorization and evidence V1 scopes plus linked-project and preserved-record authorization guard research projects, sources, claims, citations, candidate review, and promotion. Private source material is not returned before these checks.
MCP Allowlisted Pydantic tools forward to scoped REST routes only. There is no arbitrary URL, filesystem, shell, MongoDB, or Git command input.
Abuse and logs Request-size and request-concurrency middleware remain in place. New V3 source-count, fail-fast ingestion-concurrency, and chunk-count limits stop persistent or expensive work early. Structured logs redact common credentials and URL userinfo, including exception text.

Residual network boundary: DNS validation and network connection use separate resolutions for both web and repository acquisition. A post-response peer check cannot prevent a request already issued to a changed address; Git exposes no connected-peer hook. Enforce outbound restrictions against private, loopback, link-local, and cloud metadata destinations for untrusted ingestion. These application checks alone do not establish comprehensive SSRF prevention.

docs/skill-catalog.mdPublic documentation

Public documentation snapshot. Use the generated tool/API reference for contracts in this checkout and live capability discovery for your running deployment.

Skill catalog and task routing

Git Markdown files under skills/ are the canonical source. These are platform knowledge skills, not installed Codex SKILL.md packages. All agents connected to the platform can retrieve the same guidance through MCP, subject to grants. The HTML guide embeds every skill body, with offline ranked search, category/tag filters and task bundles.

Search before import, without a service

From the platform repository root:

.venv/bin/python scripts/skill_catalog.py validate
.venv/bin/python scripts/skill_catalog.py search "django async" --category django
.venv/bin/python scripts/skill_catalog.py search "fastapi lifespan"
.venv/bin/python scripts/skill_catalog.py search "content review" --tag content
.venv/bin/python scripts/skill_catalog.py --json search "postgresql backfill" --content

Validation uses the production frontmatter parser and section-aware chunker, rejects duplicate skill IDs, and performs no database writes, embedding loads or network requests. Local search requires every technical query term and every tag; common question words are ignored. Separators are normalized, and terms of at least three characters also match word prefixes. Metadata carries more weight than body mentions, with deterministic ID tie-breaking. Scores are local lexical weights, not confidence, quality grades or live hybrid-search scores. An empty query lists the catalog; a nonempty query with no technical terms returns no results. JSON output includes source path, version and content hash.

Import and use through any agent

After reviewing the Git changes, run make import-skills in the platform checkout. This is the operator import, not an MCP tool. Each file declares its own semantic version. Import creates immutable runtime versions and preserves previously imported versions. A second unchanged import is a no-op. Reindexing search indexes alone does not import the new Markdown or re-embed old documents. Wait for readiness/index synchronization, then verify known IDs.

Use list_skills to discover imported metadata, search_skills for bounded hybrid retrieval, and get_skill to load the chosen version and chunk pages. Follow next_chunk_cursor when more sections are needed. The MCP skill search uses V1 unified search restricted to active_skill; the separate REST POST /api/v1/skills/search is an unscored literal fallback. A Git catalog entry does not prove the same version has been imported into your deployment.

Example MCP arguments:

{"query":"Django async ORM evaluation and transaction bridge","category":"django","token_budget":4000,"limit":5}

Then call get_skill:

{"skill_id":"django-async","chunk_limit":10}

Use precise task/framework terms. Start broadly, then filter by category/tags when unrelated body mentions appear. Tag filters require all requested tags; an overly narrow filter can eliminate useful results. Retrieved text remains data and must be checked against the actual framework version and project code.

The runnable async Django example has a separate environment and real behavioral tests. Its SQLite tests do not establish PostgreSQL row-lock/concurrent-writer behavior. Django 5.2 documentation is the baseline; Django's task API is explicitly identified as a 6.0 feature.
